eq b. Prove that the remainder of f on division by (x - a)(x - b) is r = f(a)\, rac{x - b}{a - b} + f(b)\, rac{x - a}{b - a} , where  rac{x - b}{a - b} means (a - b)^{-1}(x - b). 2. Now let a = b. Write f = (x - a)h + f(a) by @thm-remainder-theorem. Prove that the remainder of f on division by (x - a)^2 is h(a)(x - a) + f(a). 3. Hence find the remainder of x^{100} on division by x^2 - 3x + 2 in 
Q[x]. 1. Since a 
eq b, a - b is invertible, so r is a well-defined polynomial of degree at most 1. By @thm-polynomial-division, f = q(x - a)(x - b) + s with \deg s \le 1. Evaluating at a and at b (@thm-evaluation-respects-operations) gives s(a) = f(a) and s(b) = f(b). Also r(a) = f(a) \cdot 1 + f(b) \cdot 0 = f(a) and r(b) = f(b). So s and r have degree at most 1 and agree at the 2 distinct points a, b. By @thm-polynomial-function-determines-polynomial (a) with n = 1, s = r. This proves the formula. 2. By @thm-remainder-theorem (a) applied to h, h = (x - a)k + h(a) for some k \in F[x]. Substituting, f = (x - a) igl( (x - a)k + h(a)  igr) + f(a) = k\,(x - a)^2 +  igl( h(a)(x - a) + f(a)  igr) . The last bracket has degree at most 1 < 2 = \deg (x - a)^2, so by the uniqueness in @thm-polynomial-division it is the remainder. 3. Here x^2 - 3x + 2 = (x - 1)(x - 2), with a = 1 
eq b = 2, f(1) = 1 and f(2) = 2^{100}. By (a), r = 1 \cdot  rac{x - 2}{1 - 2} + 2^{100} \cdot  rac{x - 1}{2 - 1} = (2^{100} - 1)x + (2 - 2^{100}) . As a check, r(1) = 1 and r(2) = 2^{101} - 2 + 2 - 2^{100} = 2^{100}. [C3: Equal Functions Over 
F_p] Let p be a prime and f, g \in 
F_p[x]. 1. Prove that f(c) = g(c) for every c \in 
F_p if and only if x^p - x \mid f - g in 
F_p[x]. 2. Deduce that f and its remainder on division by x^p - x define the same function 
F_p 	o 
F_p. Use this to find a polynomial of degree less than 5 that defines the same function on 
F_5 as x^7 + x. Hint for (a): @exr-polynomials-c2 and @cor-root-bound-general. 1. (⇐) Suppose f - g = (x^p - x)h. By @exr-polynomials-c2, c^p - c = 0 for every c \in 
F_p. By @thm-evaluation-respects-operations, f(c) - g(c) = (c^p - c)h(c) = 0 for every c. (⇒) Suppose f(c) = g(c) for every c \in 
F_p. Then the p distinct elements 0, 1, \dots, p - 1 of 
F_p are roots of f - g. Let P = \prod_{c \in 
F_p} (x - c). By @cor-root-bound-general, P \mid f - g. It remains to show P = x^p - x. By @exr-polynomials-c2, every c \in 
F_p is a root of x^p - x, so @cor-root-bound-general gives x^p - x = Pu for some u. Both P and x^p - x are monic of degree p (@thm-degree-of-product), so \deg u = 0, and comparing leading coefficients gives u = 1. Hence P = x^p - x, and x^p - x \mid f - g. 2. Write f = q(x^p - x) + r by @thm-polynomial-division. Then x^p - x \mid f - r, so f and r define the same function by (a). For f = x^7 + x over 
F_5: x^7 = x^2 \cdot x^5 = x^2(x^5 - x) + x^3, so x^7 + x = x^2(x^5 - x) + (x^3 + x) with \deg(x^3 + x) = 3 < 5. Hence x^3 + x defines the same function as x^7 + x on 
F_5.

title: 5.2 Ideals and Greatest Common Divisors
content:
Ideals and Greatest Common Divisors Division with remainder is now available over every field. This section uses it to answer a question about two polynomials f and g: what do all the combinations af + bg, with polynomial coefficients a and b, look like? The answer is that they are exactly the multiples of one polynomial, and that polynomial is the greatest common divisor of f and g. Along the way we meet ideals, the subsets of F[x] adapted to multiplication, and we prove that each of them is generated by a single polynomial. The Euclidean algorithm then computes the greatest common divisor and the coefficients a, b by repeated division. Throughout, F is a field. All the combinations of two polynomials Take f = x^2 - 1 and g = x^2 + x - 2 in 
Q[x], and look at the set \{ af + bg : a, b \in 
Q[x] \} of all their combinations with polynomial coefficients. It contains f (take a = 1, b = 0), g, and g - f = x - 1. Since f = (x - 1)(x + 1) and g = (x - 1)(x + 2), every combination is af + bg = (x - 1) igl( a(x + 1) + b(x + 2)  igr), a multiple of x - 1. Conversely, every multiple h(x - 1) is a combination, namely (-h)f + hg. So the set of combinations is exactly the set of multiples of x - 1. Its non-zero members of smallest degree are the non-zero scalar multiples of x - 1. By @prp-divisibility-properties (c), no non-zero constant is a multiple of x - 1, so there is nothing of degree 0. Two features of this set will carry the whole section. It is closed under addition, and it absorbs multiplication by any polynomial: if af + bg is in the set, so is h(af + bg) = (ha)f + (hb)g. Sets with these two features appear everywhere, so they get a name. Ideals In Chapter 1 we studied F[x] as a vector space and its subspaces: subsets closed under addition and under multiplication by scalars. But F[x] also has a multiplication of its own. The subsets that respect it are closed under multiplication by polynomials. Three recurring examples share this feature: - the multiples of a fixed polynomial p; - the combinations af + bg of two fixed polynomials; - the polynomials that vanish at a fixed point c: if f(c) = 0, then (hf)(c) = h(c) \cdot 0 = 0 for every h. An ideal is a set of polynomials that is closed under addition and swallows multiplication by anything. [Ideal of F\lbrack xbrack] Let F be a field. A subset I \subseteq F[x] is an ideal of F[x] if 1. I is non-empty; 2. f + g \in I for all f, g \in I; 3. hf \in I for all f \in I and every h \in F[x]. For f_1, \dots, f_k \in F[x], write \langle f_1, \dots, f_k angle \coloneqq \{ a_1 f_1 + \dots + a_k f_k : a_1, \dots, a_k \in F[x] \} . In particular \langle p angle = \{ hp : h \in F[x] \} is the set of all multiples of p. In words: (I1) rules out the empty set. (I2) says sums stay inside. (I3) is the new clause: a member of I multiplied by any polynomial, not just by a constant, is still a member. Taking h = 0 in (I3) shows 0 \in I, and taking h = -1 shows -f \in I. Taking h = c constant shows I is closed under scalar multiplication, so every ideal is a subspace of F[x] by @thm-subspace-test. The angle brackets here have nothing to do with the inner products of later chapters: \langle f, g angle is a set of polynomials, not a number. Well-definedness. We have named the set \langle f_1, \dots, f_k angle, and must check that it is an ideal. It is in fact the smallest ideal containing f_1, \dots, f_k. [The Ideal Generated by Finitely Many Polynomials] Let F be a field and f_1, \dots, f_k \in F[x], with k \ge 1. Then \langle f_1, \dots, f_k angle is an ideal of F[x] containing f_1, \dots, f_k. Moreover, every ideal J of F[x] with f_1, \dots, f_k \in J satisfies \langle f_1, \dots, f_k angle \subseteq J. Let I = \langle f_1, \dots, f_k angle. Taking a_i = 1 and a_j = 0 for j 
eq i shows f_i \in I; in particular (I1) holds. For (I2), \sum a_i f_i + \sum b_i f_i = \sum (a_i + b_i) f_i \in I. For (I3), h \sum a_i f_i = \sum (h a_i) f_i \in I, using @thm-polynomial-ring-laws in both cases. So I is an ideal. Now let J be an ideal containing every f_i. By (I3) for J, each a_i f_i \in J, and by (I2) applied k - 1 times, a_1 f_1 + \dots + a_k f_k \in J. Hence I \subseteq J. This proves the proposition. The ideal \langle f_1, \dots, f_k angle is the ideal generated by f_1, \dots, f_k. An ideal of the form \langle p angle, generated by one polynomial, is called principal. [First Ideals] Check each of the following against @def-ideal-polynomials. 1. \{0\} and F[x]; and any ideal containing a non-zero constant. 2. I_c = \{ f \in F[x] : f(c) = 0 \} for a fixed c \in F. 3. For A =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \in M_2(F), the set \{ p \in F[x] : p(A) = 0 \}. (a) \{0\} = \langle 0 angle and F[x] = \langle 1 angle are ideals by @prp-ideal-generated. They are the degenerate cases, and the second one is the one to recognize: if an ideal I contains a non-zero constant c, then 1 = c^{-1} c \in I by (I3), and then h = h \cdot 1 \in I for every h, so I = F[x]. An ideal that contains a non-zero constant is everything. (b) 0 \in I_c. If f(c) = g(c) = 0, then (f + g)(c) = 0 and (hf)(c) = h(c) f(c) = 0 for every h \in F[x], by @thm-evaluation-respects-operations. So I_c is an ideal. By @thm-remainder-theorem (b), f(c) = 0 exactly when x - c \mid f, so I_c = \langle x - c angle. (c) Call the set I. The zero polynomial is in I. If p(A) = q(A) = 0, then by @thm-polynomial-of-matrix-properties, (p + q)(A) = p(A) + q(A) = 0 and (hp)(A) = h(A)\,p(A) = h(A) \cdot 0 = 0 for every h. So I is an ideal. It contains x^2, since A^2 = 0. It contains no non-zero polynomial of degree at most 1: (a + bx)(A) =  egin{pmatrix} a & b \ 0 & a \end{pmatrix} = 0 forces a = b = 0. The same argument works for any linear operator T in place of A, with @thm-polynomial-of-operator-properties. In Chapter 8 the ideal of all polynomials killing an operator is where the minimal polynomial comes from. Now the non-example, by a minimal change. Take F[x]_{\le n} for some n \in 
N. It is non-empty, closed under addition, and closed under multiplication by constants: it is a subspace of F[x] (@exm-poly-degree-bound). But it fails (I3): x^n \in F[x]_{\le n} and x \in F[x], while x \cdot x^n = x^{n+1} 
otin F[x]_{\le n}. The exact clause that fails is “for every h \in F[x]”. Why insist on every h, and not just constants? Because the main theorem below divides a member f of I by another member d and needs the remainder f - qd to lie in I again. The quotient q is an arbitrary polynomial, so we need qd \in I. With only closure under scalars, the argument breaks, and indeed F[x]_{\le n} is not the set of multiples of any single polynomial. The name “ideal” is historical and says nothing about the definition. Do not confuse \langle f, g angle with \Span(f, g). The span uses scalar coefficients, the ideal uses polynomial coefficients. For example, \Span(x) = \{ cx : c \in F \} is a line in F[x], while \langle x angle contains x^2, x^3, \dots and is infinite-dimensional. Every ideal is a subspace, but most subspaces, such as F[x]_{\le n} or \Span(x), are not ideals. Is J = \{ f \in 
R[x] : f(1) = 0 	ext{ or } f(2) = 0 \} an ideal of 
R[x]? No. J is non-empty and satisfies (I3), since (hf)(c) = h(c)f(c). But it fails (I2): x - 1 \in J and x - 2 \in J, while their sum 2x - 3 takes the values -1 at 1 and 1 at 2, so 2x - 3 
otin J. The set with “and” in place of “or” is an ideal. Every ideal is generated by one polynomial The payoff of the definition is that ideals of F[x] are very simple: each one is the set of multiples of a single polynomial. The proof is the argument of the opening example, made general. We have met it before for integers, in @lem-bezout-integers, where the smallest positive combination ax + ny turned out to divide a and n. [Every Ideal of F\lbrack xbrack Is Principal] Let F be a field and I an ideal of F[x]. If I 
eq \{0\}, there is exactly one monic polynomial d with I = \langle d angle. Moreover, d is the unique monic polynomial of least degree in I. Pick a non-zero d \in I of smallest degree, made monic. Every multiple of d is in I by (I3). For the other inclusion, divide any f \in I by d: the remainder r = f - qd lies in I and has degree smaller than \deg d. Minimality leaves only one option, r = 0. Uniqueness is mutual divisibility of monic polynomials. Suppose I 
eq \{0\}. The degrees of the non-zero elements of I form a non-empty set of natural numbers, so by @thm-well-ordering it has a least element m. Choose g \in I with \deg g = m, and let c be its leading coefficient. Put d = c^{-1} g. Then d \in I by (I3), and d is monic of degree m. (⊇) For every h \in F[x], hd \in I by (I3). Hence \langle d angle \subseteq I. (⊆) Let f \in I. By @thm-polynomial-division, f = qd + r with \deg r < m. By (I3), -qd \in I, and by (I2), r = f + (-qd) \in I. If r 
eq 0, then r is a non-zero element of I of degree less than m, contradicting the choice of m. Hence r = 0, so f = qd \in \langle d angle. Therefore I = \langle d angle. For uniqueness, let d' be monic with I = \langle d' angle. Then d \in \langle d' angle and d' \in \langle d angle, so d' \mid d and d \mid d'. Both are monic, so d = d' by @prp-divisibility-properties (d). Finally, let e \in I be monic of least degree m. Then d \mid e, so e = ud with \deg u = 0 by @thm-degree-of-product, and comparing leading coefficients gives u = 1. Hence e = d. This proves the theorem. For I = \{0\} the only generator is 0, since \langle p angle contains p. So every ideal of F[x] is principal, with a canonical generator: 0 for the zero ideal, and the monic polynomial of least degree otherwise. The named move is: the smallest-degree element of an ideal generates it. In @exm-ideals-polynomials (c), the ideal contains x^2 and nothing non-zero of smaller degree, so it equals \langle x^2 angle. The theorem also turns divisibility into containment. For p, q \in F[x], \langle p angle \subseteq \langle q angle \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad q \mid p , because \langle p angle \subseteq \langle q angle holds exactly when p \in \langle q angle, by @prp-ideal-generated. The bigger the ideal, the smaller the generator. Find the monic generator of \langle x^2 - 1, \; x^3 - 1 angle \subseteq 
Q[x] by finding an element of small degree in it. The ideal contains (x^3 - 1) - x(x^2 - 1) = x - 1. Both generators are multiples of x - 1, since x^2 - 1 = (x - 1)(x + 1) and x^3 - 1 = (x - 1)(x^2 + x + 1), so every combination is a multiple of x - 1 by @prp-divisibility-properties (b). A non-zero constant is not a multiple of x - 1, so x - 1 has least degree in the ideal. By @thm-ideals-principal, the ideal is \langle x - 1 angle. The greatest common divisor Apply @thm-ideals-principal to the ideal \langle f, g angle of all combinations. It has a canonical generator, and in the opening example that generator, x - 1, was a common divisor of f and g. A naive attempt to define “the greatest common divisor” as “a common divisor of largest degree” runs into a problem at once: x - 1, 2x - 2 and -	frac13 x + 	frac13 are all common divisors of x^2 - 1 and x^2 + x - 2 of the largest possible degree. Degree cannot tell associates apart, and it also does not say how the common divisors relate to each other. The generator of the ideal fixes both problems. The gcd of f and g is the monic polynomial whose multiples are exactly the combinations of f and g. [Greatest Common Divisor] Let F be a field and f, g \in F[x]. If f and g are not both zero, the greatest common divisor \gcd(f, g) is the unique monic polynomial d \in F[x] with \langle f, g angle = \langle d angle . We set \gcd(0, 0) = 0. In words: form the ideal of all combinations af + bg with a, b \in F[x]; it is generated by one polynomial; take the monic one. The definition refers to F[x] twice, in the coefficients a, b and in the generator d, so at first sight the gcd depends on the field. We show below that it does not change when the field is enlarged. Well-definedness. By @prp-ideal-generated, \langle f, g angle is an ideal. If f and g are not both zero, it contains a non-zero element, so by @thm-ideals-principal there is exactly one monic d with \langle f, g angle = \langle d angle. The convention \gcd(0, 0) = 0 keeps the equation \langle f, g angle = \langle \gcd(f, g) angle true in the remaining case. The definition is symmetric: \gcd(f, g) = \gcd(g, f). [First Greatest Common Divisors] 1. Let f 
eq 0 have leading coefficient a. Find \gcd(f, 0) and \gcd(f, c) for a non-zero constant c. 2. Find \gcd(x^2 - 1, x^2 + x - 2) in 
Q[x]. 3. Find \gcd(x^2 + 1, x + 1) in 
Q[x] and in 
F_2[x]. (a) \langle f, 0 angle = \{ af : a \in F[x] \} = \langle f angle = \langle a^{-1} f angle, and a^{-1} f is monic, so \gcd(f, 0) = a^{-1} f, the monic associate of f. This degenerate case shows why the gcd must be made monic: f itself generates the ideal too, but is not the canonical choice. Next, \langle f, c angle contains the non-zero constant c, so it is F[x] = \langle 1 angle by @exm-ideals-polynomials (a). Hence \gcd(f, c) = 1. (b) The opening example showed \langle x^2 - 1, x^2 + x - 2 angle = \langle x - 1 angle, and x - 1 is monic. So the gcd is x - 1. (c) In 
Q[x]: dividing, x^2 + 1 = (x - 1)(x + 1) + 2. So 2 = (x^2 + 1) - (x - 1)(x + 1) lies in the ideal, which is therefore 
Q[x] by @exm-ideals-polynomials (a). Hence \gcd = 1. In 
F_2[x]: x^2 + 1 = (x + 1)^2, so x^2 + 1 \in \langle x + 1 angle, and \langle x^2 + 1, x + 1 angle = \langle x + 1 angle by @prp-ideal-generated. Hence \gcd = x + 1. The symbols are the same, but 
F_2 is not a field containing 
Q, so the two answers need not agree. For a non-example by minimal change, keep (b) but replace x - 1 by the associate 3x - 3. It is still a common divisor of largest degree and still generates the ideal, but it is not \gcd(x^2 - 1, x^2 + x - 2): the clause “monic” fails. Or keep “monic” but lower the degree: 1 is a monic common divisor, and it does not generate the ideal, since 1 
otin \langle x - 1 angle. Why define the gcd through the ideal, rather than as “the largest common divisor”? Because the ideal definition delivers three things at once: existence and uniqueness (from @thm-ideals-principal), the fact that the gcd is a combination of f and g, and the fact that it is “greatest” in the strongest sense, namely that every common divisor divides it. Here is the last point. [Characterization of the gcd] Let F be a field, f, g \in F[x], and d = \gcd(f, g). 1. d \mid f and d \mid g. 2. If h \in F[x] satisfies h \mid f and h \mid g, then h \mid d. 3. If f, g are not both zero, then d is the only monic polynomial with properties (a) and (b). (a) f = 1 \cdot f + 0 \cdot g \in \langle f, g angle = \langle d angle, so d \mid f. Similarly d \mid g. (b) Since d \in \langle d angle = \langle f, g angle, there are a, b \in F[x] with d = af + bg. If h \mid f and h \mid g, then h \mid af + bg = d by @prp-divisibility-properties (b). (c) Let e be monic with properties (a) and (b). Since d is a common divisor of f and g, property (b) for e gives d \mid e. Since e is a common divisor, property (b) for d gives e \mid d. Both are monic (e by assumption, and d by @def-gcd-polynomials, since f, g are not both zero), so d = e by @prp-divisibility-properties (d). This proves the theorem. So \gcd(f, g) is a common divisor that every common divisor divides. If f, g are not both zero, then d 
eq 0, and by @prp-divisibility-properties (c) every common divisor has degree at most \deg d; “greatest” is true for degrees as well. The proof of (b) used one fact that deserves its own statement, because it is the most useful property of the gcd. [Bézout’s Identity for Polynomials] Let F be a field and f, g \in F[x]. Then there exist a, b \in F[x] with \gcd(f, g) = af + bg . By @def-gcd-polynomials, \gcd(f, g) \in \langle \gcd(f, g) angle = \langle f, g angle, and the elements of \langle f, g angle are exactly the combinations af + bg. The coefficients are not unique: if d = af + bg, then also d = (a + g)f + (b - f)g. Bézout’s identity is the polynomial version of @lem-bezout-integers, and it will be the tool behind the Chinese Remainder Theorem and the splitting of kernels later in this chapter. The Euclidean algorithm The definition tells us what the gcd is, but not how to find it. Factoring f and g is usually hard. Division is easy, and one observation turns division into an algorithm: dividing does not change the ideal. [Dividing Does Not Change the Ideal] Let F be a field and f, g, q, r \in F[x] with f = qg + r. Then \langle f, g angle = \langle g, r angle. Consequently \gcd(f, g) = \gcd(g, r). (⊇) The ideal \langle f, g angle contains g, and r = f + (-q)g by (I2) and (I3). By @prp-ideal-generated, \langle g, r angle \subseteq \langle f, g angle. (⊆) The ideal \langle g, r angle contains g and f = qg + r. By @prp-ideal-generated, \langle f, g angle \subseteq \langle g, r angle. Hence the two ideals are equal. The gcd is the canonical generator of the ideal (@def-gcd-polynomials), and f, g are both zero exactly when g, r are, so \gcd(f, g) = \gcd(g, r). Now divide repeatedly. Each division replaces the pair (f, g) by (g, r), a pair with the same gcd and a smaller second entry. [Euclidean Algorithm] Let F be a field and f, g \in F[x] with g 
eq 0. Put r_{-1} = f and r_0 = g. As long as r_k 
eq 0, divide r_{k-1} by r_k (@thm-polynomial-division): r_{k-1} = q_{k+1} r_k + r_{k+1}, \qquad \deg r_{k+1} < \deg r_k . Then: 1. the process stops: there is an index n with 0 \le n \le \deg g such that r_n 
eq 0 and r_{n+1} = 0; 2. if c is the leading coefficient of this last non-zero remainder r_n, then \gcd(f, g) = c^{-1} r_n. Two things to see. The degrees \deg r_0 > \deg r_1 > \deg r_2 > \cdots strictly decrease, and natural numbers cannot decrease forever, so some remainder is 0. By @lem-euclid-step, the ideal \langle r_{k-1}, r_k angle never changes along the way; at the end it is \langle r_n, 0 angle = \langle r_n angle, and making r_n monic gives the gcd. (a) As long as r_1, \dots, r_j are all non-zero, their degrees are natural numbers with \deg g = \deg r_0 > \deg r_1 > \dots > \deg r_j \ge 0. So r_1, \dots, r_j are j distinct values in \{0, 1, \dots, \deg g - 1\}, and j \le \deg g. Hence the remainders cannot all be non-zero for j = \deg g + 1: there is a first index n + 1 with r_{n+1} = 0, and n \le \deg g. Also n \ge 0 since r_0 = g 
eq 0. (b) We show by induction on k that \langle r_{k-1}, r_k angle = \langle f, g angle for k = 0, 1, \dots, n + 1. For k = 0 this is the definition of r_{-1}, r_0. If it holds for some k \le n, then r_{k-1} = q_{k+1} r_k + r_{k+1}, and @lem-euclid-step gives \langle r_k, r_{k+1} angle = \langle r_{k-1}, r_k angle = \langle f, g angle. For k = n + 1 this reads \langle f, g angle = \langle r_n, 0 angle = \langle r_n angle. Since c 
eq 0, \langle r_n angle = \langle c^{-1} r_n angle, and c^{-1} r_n is monic. Because g 
eq 0, @def-gcd-polynomials gives \gcd(f, g) = c^{-1} r_n. This proves the theorem. If g = 0, no division is needed: \gcd(f, 0) is the monic associate of f (or 0), as in @exm-gcd-first (a). The algorithm also produces Bézout coefficients. Each remainder is a combination of the previous two, r_{k+1} = r_{k-1} - q_{k+1} r_k, so by induction each remainder is a combination of f and g. Keeping track of the coefficients gives the following procedure. Extended Euclidean algorithm. Input: f, g \in F[x] with g 
eq 0. 1. Set (r_{-1}, a_{-1}, b_{-1}) = (f, 1, 0) and (r_0, a_0, b_0) = (g, 0, 1). 2. For k = 0, 1, 2, \dots, as long as r_k 
eq 0: divide r_{k-1} = q_{k+1} r_k + r_{k+1}, and set a_{k+1} = a_{k-1} - q_{k+1} a_k, \qquad b_{k+1} = b_{k-1} - q_{k+1} b_k . 3. When r_{n+1} = 0, let c be the leading coefficient of r_n. Output \gcd(f, g) = c^{-1} r_n and the coefficients a = c^{-1} a_n, b = c^{-1} b_n. The invariant r_k = a_k f + b_k g holds for k = -1, 0 by the choice in step 1. If it holds for k - 1 and k, then r_{k+1} = r_{k-1} - q_{k+1} r_k = (a_{k-1} - q_{k+1} a_k) f + (b_{k-1} - q_{k+1} b_k) g = a_{k+1} f + b_{k+1} g . So at the end \gcd(f, g) = c^{-1} r_n = af + bg. By hand, it is often quicker to write each division as “remainder = \dots” and substitute backwards, which is the same computation. [The Euclidean Algorithm with Back-Substitution] In 
Q[x], let f = x^4 - x^3 - 3x^2 + x + 2 and g = x^3 - 2x - 1. Find \gcd(f, g) and polynomials a, b with \gcd(f, g) = af + bg. Divisions. First divide f by g. The leading terms give x, and f - xg = -x^3 - x^2 + 2x + 2; then -1, and adding g leaves -x^2 + 1. So f = (x - 1)\,g + r_1, \qquad r_1 = 1 - x^2 . Next divide g by r_1. The leading terms give x^3 / (-x^2) = -x, and g - (-x) r_1 = x^3 - 2x - 1 + x - x^3 = -x - 1. So g = (-x)\, r_1 + r_2, \qquad r_2 = -x - 1 . Next divide r_1 by r_2. Since (x - 1)(-x - 1) = -x^2 + 1, r_1 = (x - 1)\, r_2 + 0 . The last non-zero remainder is r_2 = -x - 1, with leading coefficient -1. By @thm-euclidean-algorithm, \gcd(f, g) = x + 1. Back-substitution. From the first two divisions, r_1 = f - (x - 1) g, \qquad r_2 = g + x\, r_1 . Substituting the first into the second, r_2 = g + x igl( f - (x - 1) g  igr) = x f + (1 + x - x^2)\, g . Multiplying by c^{-1} = -1, x + 1 = (-x)\, f + (x^2 - x - 1)\, g . In the notation of the algorithm, (a_1, b_1) = (1, 1 - x) and (a_2, b_2) = (x, 1 + x - x^2). Checks. Expanding, -x(x^4 - x^3 - 3x^2 + x + 2) = -x^5 + x^4 + 3x^3 - x^2 - 2x and (x^2 - x - 1)(x^3 - 2x - 1) = x^5 - x^4 - 3x^3 + x^2 + 3x + 1, which sum to x + 1. As an independent check that x + 1 divides both, f(-1) = 1 + 1 - 3 - 1 + 2 = 0 and g(-1) = -1 + 2 - 1 = 0, so @thm-remainder-theorem applies. Coprime polynomials The most important value a gcd can take is 1. Then f and g share no non-constant factor, and Bézout’s identity writes 1 itself as a combination. Coprime Polynomials Let F be a field. Polynomials f, g \in F[x] are coprime (or relatively prime) over F if \gcd(f, g) = 1. [Coprime Means 1 Is a Combination] Let F be a field and f, g \in F[x]. Then f and g are coprime if and only if there exist a, b \in F[x] with af + bg = 1. (⇒) This is @cor-bezout-polynomials with \gcd(f, g) = 1. (⇐) If af + bg = 1, then 1 \in \langle f, g angle, so \langle f, g angle = F[x] = \langle 1 angle by @exm-ideals-polynomials (a). In particular f, g are not both zero, and the monic generator is 1. Hence \gcd(f, g) = 1. Examples: for distinct c, c' \in F, the polynomials x - c and x - c' are coprime, since (c' - c)^{-1}(x - c) - (c' - c)^{-1}(x - c') = (c' - c)^{-1}(c' - c) = 1 . A non-zero constant is coprime to every polynomial (@exm-gcd-first (a)). The polynomial 0 is coprime only to the non-zero constants. Non-example: x^2 - 1 and x + 1 are not coprime, since x + 1 divides both, so x + 1 \mid \gcd by @thm-gcd-properties (b), and the gcd has degree at least 1. Coprimality is what lets a divisor pass through a product. [A Coprime Factor Can Be Canceled] Let F be a field and p, q, r \in F[x]. If p \mid qr and \gcd(p, q) = 1, then p \mid r. By @prp-coprime-criterion, there are a, b \in F[x] with ap + bq = 1. Multiplying by r, r = (ar)p + b(qr). Here p \mid p and p \mid qr by hypothesis, so p \mid r by @prp-divisibility-properties (b). This proves the theorem. The coprimality hypothesis cannot be dropped. Take p = x^2 and q = r = x. Then p \mid qr = x^2, but p 
mid r, since \deg x^2 > \deg x (@prp-divisibility-properties (c)). Here \gcd(p, q) = x 
eq 1: part of p is absorbed by q and part by r. In the next section, @thm-coprime-divides-product becomes Euclid’s lemma for irreducible polynomials, which is the heart of unique factorization. Least common multiples, briefly. For f, g \in F[x], the intersection \langle f angle \cap \langle g angle is again an ideal: it contains 0, so (I1) holds, and (I2) and (I3) hold in each of \langle f angle and \langle g angle, hence in the intersection. Its members are the common multiples of f and g. [Least Common Multiple] Let F be a field and f, g \in F[x]. The least common multiple \operatorname{lcm}(f, g) is the monic generator of the ideal \langle f angle \cap \langle g angle if this ideal is non-zero, and 0 otherwise. Exactly as for the gcd, \operatorname{lcm}(f, g) is a common multiple of f and g that divides every common multiple, by @thm-ideals-principal. If f = 0 or g = 0, the only common multiple is 0; otherwise fg is a non-zero common multiple. For monic f and g, \gcd(f, g) \cdot \operatorname{lcm}(f, g) = fg; this is proved in Exercise C3. For example, in 
Q[x], \gcd(x^2 - 1, x^2 + x - 2) = x - 1, so \operatorname{lcm}(x^2 - 1, x^2 + x - 2) = (x - 1)(x + 1)(x + 2). The gcd does not depend on the field A polynomial with rational coefficients is also a polynomial with real and with complex coefficients. Its gcd with another rational polynomial can be computed in 
Q[x], 
R[x] or 
C[x], and the definition does not obviously give the same answer, because the coefficients a, b in \langle f, g angle range over a larger set. The Euclidean algorithm shows the answers agree. Recall that a subfield K of a field L is a subset closed under the field operations (@def-restriction-of-scalars); then K[x] \subseteq L[x], with the same addition and multiplication. [The gcd Is the Same Over a Larger Field] Let K be a subfield of a field L, and let f, g \in K[x]. Then the greatest common divisor of f and g computed in K[x] equals the one computed in L[x]. In particular, f and g are coprime over K if and only if they are coprime over L. If g = 0, both gcds are the monic associate of f (or 0), by @exm-gcd-first (a), and this does not depend on the field. Let g 
eq 0, and run the Euclidean algorithm in K[x]: r_{k-1} = q_{k+1} r_k + r_{k+1} with \deg r_{k+1} < \deg r_k, all in K[x]. Each of these equations also holds in L[x], with the same degree condition. By the uniqueness in @thm-polynomial-division over L, they are exactly the divisions that the algorithm performs in L[x]. So both runs produce the same last non-zero remainder r_n, and @thm-euclidean-algorithm gives the same gcd c^{-1} r_n in both. This proves the proposition. The gcd does not see the field, but factorization does. Over 
Q, the polynomial x^2 - 2 has no root, by @thm-sqrt2-irrational, so it has no factor x - c with c \in 
Q (@thm-remainder-theorem). Over 
R it factors as (x - \sqrt2)(x + \sqrt2). Yet \gcd(x^2 - 2, x^2 - 2x), say, is the same over 
Q and over 
R. So “coprime” is a robust notion, while “cannot be factored” depends on the field; the next section makes the second notion precise. A useful consequence: if f, g \in 
Q[x] are coprime over 
Q, then they have no common root in 
C. Indeed, af + bg = 1 with a, b \in 
Q[x] \subseteq 
C[x], and evaluating at a common root z would give 0 = 1 by @thm-evaluation-respects-operations. So common complex roots can be detected by a computation that never leaves 
Q. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. Define an ideal of F[x]. 2. State the theorem describing all ideals of F[x]. 3. Determine whether the following statement is true: “for all f, g \in F[x], \Span(f, g) = \langle f, g angle.” Justify your answer. 4. Is \gcd(2x - 2, 4x^2 - 4) = 2x - 2 in 
Q[x]? Justify your answer. 5. Determine whether the following statement is true: “if af + bg = x - 1 for some a, b \in 
Q[x], then \gcd(f, g) = x - 1.” Justify your answer. 6. Name an algorithm that computes \gcd(f, g) using only division with remainder (@thm-polynomial-division). 1. A subset I \subseteq F[x] is an ideal if it is non-empty, f + g \in I for all f, g \in I, and hf \in I for all f \in I and every h \in F[x] (@def-ideal-polynomials). 2. If I 
eq \{0\} is an ideal of F[x], there is exactly one monic d with I = \langle d angle, namely the monic polynomial of least degree in I (@thm-ideals-principal). 3. False. Take f = g = x. Then \Span(x, x) = \{ cx : c \in F \} does not contain x^2, while x^2 = x \cdot x \in \langle x, x angle. The span allows only scalar coefficients. 4. No. The gcd is monic by definition. Since 4x^2 - 4 = (2x - 2)(2x + 2), we have \langle 2x - 2, 4x^2 - 4 angle = \langle 2x - 2 angle = \langle x - 1 angle, so the gcd is x - 1. 5. False. Take f = x and g = x - 1, with a = 0, b = 1. Then af + bg = x - 1, but \gcd(x, x - 1) = 1, because x - (x - 1) = 1 (@prp-coprime-criterion). What is true is that \gcd(f, g) divides every combination af + bg, by @thm-gcd-properties (a) and @prp-divisibility-properties (b). 6. The Euclidean algorithm (@thm-euclidean-algorithm). B. Practice [B1: gcd and Bézout Coefficients of Two Cubics] In 
Q[x], let f = x^3 + x^2 + x + 1 and g = x^3 + x + 2. Use the Euclidean algorithm to find d = \gcd(f, g) and polynomials a, b \in 
Q[x] with d = af + bg. Hence find all complex numbers that are roots of both f and g. Divide f by g: f = 1 \cdot g + r_1 with r_1 = f - g = x^2 - 1. Divide g by r_1: x \cdot r_1 = x^3 - x, and g - x r_1 = 2x + 2, so g = x\, r_1 + r_2 with r_2 = 2x + 2. Divide r_1 by r_2: x^2 - 1 = 	frac12 (x - 1)(2x + 2) + 0. The last non-zero remainder is r_2 = 2x + 2, with leading coefficient 2, so d = x + 1 by @thm-euclidean-algorithm. Back-substituting, r_2 = g - x r_1 = g - x(f - g) = -x f + (1 + x) g. Dividing by 2, x + 1 = \Bigl( - rac{x}{2} \Bigr) f +  rac{x + 1}{2}\, g . Check: -	frac{x}{2}(x^3 + x^2 + x + 1) + 	frac{x+1}{2}(x^3 + x + 2) = 	frac12 igl( -x^4 - x^3 - x^2 - x + x^4 + x^3 + x^2 + 3x + 2  igr) = x + 1. Hence: let z \in 
C. If f(z) = g(z) = 0, then evaluating the identity above in 
C (@thm-evaluation-respects-operations) gives z + 1 = 0. Conversely, x + 1 divides f and g (@thm-gcd-properties (a)), so -1 is a root of both. Therefore -1 is the only common complex root. [B2: Ideal or Not?] Determine which of the following subsets of 
R[x] are ideals. For each ideal, find its monic generator. Justify your answers. 1. S_1 = \{ f \in 
R[x] : f(1) = f(-1) \}. 2. S_2 = \{ f \in 
R[x] : f(0) = 0 	ext{ and } f(1) = 0 \}. 3. S_3 = \{ f \in 
R[x] : \deg f \ge 3 \} \cup \{0\}. 4. S_4 = \{ f \in 
R[x] : f(i) = 0 \}, where f(i) means the value at i \in 
C of f regarded as a complex polynomial. 1. Not an ideal. S_1 is a subspace, and 1 \in S_1. But x \cdot 1 = x has x(1) = 1 
eq -1 = x(-1), so x 
otin S_1, and (I3) fails. 2. An ideal. The argument of @exm-ideals-polynomials (b), applied at both points, gives (I1)–(I3). If f \in S_2, then 0 and 1 are distinct roots of f, so x(x - 1) \mid f by @cor-root-bound-general. Conversely every multiple of x^2 - x vanishes at 0 and 1. Hence S_2 = \langle x^2 - x angle, with monic generator x^2 - x. 3. Not an ideal. x^3 \in S_3 and -x^3 + x \in S_3, but their sum x has degree 1 and is non-zero, so (I2) fails. 4. An ideal: evaluation at i respects sums and products (@thm-evaluation-respects-operations over 
C), so the argument of @exm-ideals-polynomials (b) applies. It contains x^2 + 1. A non-zero element of degree at most 1 would be a + bx with a, b \in 
R not both zero and a + bi = 0, which is impossible since the real and imaginary parts give a = b = 0. So the least degree of a non-zero element is 2. If d is the monic generator (@thm-ideals-principal), then \deg d = 2 and d \mid x^2 + 1, so x^2 + 1 = ud with u constant, and comparing leading coefficients gives u = 1. Hence S_4 = \langle x^2 + 1 angle. [B3: The gcd of x^m - 1 and x^n - 1] Let F be a field. For integers m, n \ge 0, not both zero, let \gcd(m, n) denote the largest positive integer dividing both. 1. For m \ge n \ge 1, verify that x^m - 1 = x^{m-n}(x^n - 1) + (x^{m-n} - 1). 2. Prove that \gcd(x^m - 1, x^n - 1) = x^{\gcd(m, n)} - 1 in F[x] for all m, n \ge 0 not both zero, where x^0 - 1 = 0. 3. Hence compute \gcd(x^{12} - 1, x^{18} - 1). Hint for (b): @thm-euclidean-algorithm, run on the exponents. 1. Expanding, x^{m-n}(x^n - 1) + x^{m-n} - 1 = x^m - x^{m-n} + x^{m-n} - 1 = x^m - 1. 2. We use strong induction on s = m + n \ge 1 (@thm-strong-induction). If n = 0, then m \ge 1, \gcd(m, 0) = m, and \gcd(x^m - 1, 0) is the monic associate of x^m - 1, which is x^m - 1 itself (@exm-gcd-first (a)). The case m = 0 is the same, since both gcds are symmetric. Now let m, n \ge 1; by symmetry we may assume m \ge n. By (a) and @lem-euclid-step, \gcd(x^m - 1, x^n - 1) = \gcd(x^n - 1, x^{m-n} - 1) . The pair (n, m - n) is not both zero and has sum m < m + n, so by the induction hypothesis the right side is x^{\gcd(n, m - n)} - 1. Finally, \gcd(n, m - n) = \gcd(m, n): if k \mid m and k \mid n, then k \mid m - n; and if k \mid n and k \mid m - n, then k \mid (m - n) + n = m. So the two pairs have the same positive common divisors, and the same largest one. This completes the induction. 3. By (b), \gcd(x^{12} - 1, x^{18} - 1) = x^{\gcd(12, 18)} - 1 = x^6 - 1. C. Going deeper [C1: Polynomials Vanishing on a Set] Let F be a field and S \subseteq F non-empty. Put I(S) = \{ f \in F[x] : f(s) = 0 	ext{ for all } s \in S \}. 1. Prove that I(S) is an ideal of F[x]. 2. Suppose S = \{ s_1, \dots, s_k \} is finite, with the s_i distinct. Prove that I(S) = \langle (x - s_1) \cdots (x - s_k) angle. 3. Suppose S is infinite. Prove that I(S) = \{0\}. 4. Deduce from (b) and @exr-division-c3 that I(
F_p) = \langle x^p - x angle for every prime p. 1. The zero polynomial vanishes everywhere, so I(S) 
eq \varnothing. If f, g \in I(S) and h \in F[x], then for every s \in S, @thm-evaluation-respects-operations gives (f + g)(s) = 0 + 0 = 0 and (hf)(s) = h(s) \cdot 0 = 0. So (I2) and (I3) hold. 2. Let P = (x - s_1) \cdots (x - s_k). Every multiple hP vanishes at each s_i, since P(s_i) = 0; so \langle P angle \subseteq I(S). Conversely, if f \in I(S), then s_1, \dots, s_k are distinct roots of f, and @cor-root-bound-general gives P \mid f. Hence I(S) = \langle P angle, and since P is monic, it is the monic generator. 3. Let f \in I(S), and suppose f 
eq 0. Since S is infinite, it contains \deg f + 1 distinct elements, all roots of f. This contradicts @cor-root-bound-general. Hence f = 0. 4. By (b), I(
F_p) = \langle P angle with P = \prod_{c \in 
F_p} (x - c). The solution of @exr-division-c3 (a) showed P = x^p - x. Hence I(
F_p) = \langle x^p - x angle. [C2: A Non-Principal Ideal in Two Variables] A polynomial in two variables over F is a finite sum P = \sum_{i, j} a_{ij} x^i y^j with a_{ij} \in F, only finitely many non-zero; two are equal when all coefficients agree. They are added coefficient by coefficient and multiplied by expanding and collecting, and the set F[x, y] of all of them satisfies the laws of @thm-polynomial-ring-laws, which you may use. Ideals of F[x, y] and \langle P_1, \dots, P_k angle are defined exactly as in @def-ideal-polynomials, and @prp-ideal-generated holds with the same proof. For P 
eq 0, let \deg_y P be the largest j with a_{ij} 
eq 0 for some i, and define \deg_x P similarly. 1. Prove that \deg_y(PQ) = \deg_y P + \deg_y Q for non-zero P, Q \in F[x, y]. By symmetry the same holds for \deg_x. 2. Show that \langle x, y angle consists of the polynomials whose constant coefficient a_{00} is 0. 3. Prove that \langle x, y angle 
eq \langle D angle for every D \in F[x, y]. 4. Explain precisely which step of the proof of @thm-ideals-principal has no analogue in F[x, y]. Hint for (a): write P = \sum_{j} p_j(x) y^j with p_j \in F[x], and use @cor-polynomial-no-zero-divisors. 1. Group terms by the power of y: P = \sum_{j=0}^{s} p_j y^j and Q = \sum_{j=0}^{t} q_j y^j with p_j, q_j \in F[x], s = \deg_y P, t = \deg_y Q, so p_s 
eq 0 and q_t 
eq 0. Expanding, the terms of PQ with y-power greater than s + t are all zero, and the terms with y^{s+t} come only from p_s y^s \cdot q_t y^t, giving (p_s q_t) y^{s+t}. By @cor-polynomial-no-zero-divisors, p_s q_t 
eq 0 in F[x], so some coefficient of x^i y^{s+t} in PQ is non-zero. Hence \deg_y(PQ) = s + t. 2. Every Ax + By has constant coefficient 0, since each term of Ax and By involves x or y to a positive power. Conversely, if a_{00} = 0, then every term a_{ij}x^iy^j with i \ge 1 is a multiple of x, and every term with i = 0, j \ge 1 is a multiple of y. Grouping them, P = Ax + By for some A, B \in F[x, y]. 3. Suppose \langle x, y angle = \langle D angle. Since x \in \langle D angle, x = HD for some H, so D 
eq 0 and H 
eq 0. By (a), 0 = \deg_y x = \deg_y H + \deg_y D, so \deg_y D = 0: D involves no y. Similarly y = KD gives \deg_x D = 0. So D is a non-zero constant. But D \in \langle x, y angle, so its constant coefficient is 0 by (b), that is, D = 0. This contradiction shows that \langle x, y angle is not principal. 4. The proof of @thm-ideals-principal picks a non-zero d \in I of least degree, writes each f \in I as f = qd + r with r smaller than d by @thm-polynomial-division, notes r = f - qd \in I, and concludes r = 0 from minimality. Measure size in F[x, y] by the total degree, the largest i + j with a_{ij} 
eq 0. Choosing d still works: by (b), every non-zero element of \langle x, y angle has total degree at least 1, and those of total degree 1 are the ax + by with (a, b) 
eq (0, 0). Let d be any of them. Then \langle d angle \subseteq \langle x, y angle by (I3), and the inclusion is strict by (c), so some f \in \langle x, y angle is not a multiple of d. For this f and every Q \in F[x, y], the element R = f - Qd lies in \langle x, y angle and is non-zero, so its total degree is at least 1, the total degree of d. So no remainder smaller than d exists: the step with no analogue is division with remainder, the appeal to @thm-polynomial-division. Concretely, for d = x and f = y, every term of Qx contains x, so the term y survives in y - Qx. The underlying reason is that, viewed as a polynomial in y with coefficients in F[x], the leading coefficient x of d is not invertible in F[x], which is exactly the obstacle of the warning after @thm-polynomial-division. [C3: gcd Times lcm] Let F be a field and f, g \in F[x] monic. Put d = \gcd(f, g) and write f = d f_1, g = d g_1 with f_1, g_1 \in F[x]. 1. Prove that \gcd(f_1, g_1) = 1. 2. Prove that m = d f_1 g_1 is a monic common multiple of f and g that divides every common multiple of f and g. 3. Deduce that \operatorname{lcm}(f, g) = d f_1 g_1, and hence \gcd(f, g) \cdot \operatorname{lcm}(f, g) = fg. 4. Show by an example in 
Q[x] that the formula in (c) fails if f and g are not monic. Hint for (b): use @thm-coprime-divides-product. 1. The quotients exist by @thm-gcd-properties (a), and d 
eq 0 since f 
eq 0. By @cor-bezout-polynomials, d = af + bg = d(af_1 + bg_1). Canceling d 
eq 0 (@cor-polynomial-no-zero-divisors (2)) gives af_1 + bg_1 = 1, so \gcd(f_1, g_1) = 1 by @prp-coprime-criterion. 2. Comparing leading coefficients in f = d f_1 with f, d monic shows f_1 is monic; likewise g_1. So m is monic, and m = f g_1 = g f_1 is a common multiple. Let M be any common multiple, say M = fu. Since g \mid M, write M = gv. Then d f_1 u = d g_1 v, and canceling d gives f_1 u = g_1 v, so g_1 \mid f_1 u. By (a) and @thm-coprime-divides-product, g_1 \mid u, say u = g_1 w. Hence M = f g_1 w = m w, and m \mid M. 3. By (b), m \in \langle f angle \cap \langle g angle, and every element of this ideal is a multiple of m. So \langle f angle \cap \langle g angle = \langle m angle, and m is monic, hence \operatorname{lcm}(f, g) = m by @def-lcm-polynomials and @thm-ideals-principal. Then \gcd(f, g) \cdot \operatorname{lcm}(f, g) = d \cdot d f_1 g_1 = (d f_1)(d g_1) = fg. 4. Take f = g = 2x. Then \gcd(f, g) = x and \operatorname{lcm}(f, g) = x, both monic, so their product is x^2, while fg = 4x^2. In general the two sides differ by the product of the leading coefficients.

title: 5.3 Irreducible Polynomials and Unique Factorization
content:
Irreducible Polynomials and Unique Factorization Every integer n \ge 2 is a product of primes, and Chapter 0 remarked that the convention “1 is not prime” is what makes such factorizations unique. Polynomials over a field behave the same way, with irreducible polynomials in the role of primes and non-zero constants in the role of \pm 1. This section defines irreducible polynomials, proves Euclid’s lemma from the gcd machinery of the previous section, and proves that every non-constant polynomial factors into irreducibles in exactly one way. The catch is that “irreducible” depends on the field: the same polynomial may factor over 
R but not over 
Q, or over 
F_5 but not over 
F_3. So we also collect tools for deciding irreducibility over specific fields: roots in low degree, the Rational Root Theorem, and Eisenstein’s criterion. Throughout, F is a field. Irreducible polynomials For integers, the building blocks are the primes: integers p \ge 2 whose only positive divisors are 1 and p (@def-divisibility-prime). To transplant this to F[x], recall from the first section that every non-zero constant divides every polynomial, and that multiplying by a non-zero constant changes nothing for divisibility. So the trivial divisors of p are the non-zero constants and the associates cp. A building block should have no others. An irreducible polynomial is a non-constant polynomial that cannot be split into two factors of smaller degree. [Irreducible Polynomial] Let F be a field. A polynomial p \in F[x] is irreducible over F if 1. p is non-constant, that is, \deg p \ge 1; and 2. whenever p = gh with g, h \in F[x], one of g, h is a constant. A non-constant polynomial that is not irreducible is reducible over F. In words: condition (1) excludes 0 and the non-zero constants. Condition (2) says every factorization of p is trivial: one factor is a constant, which is non-zero because p 
eq 0, and the other is then an associate of p. The phrase over F is part of the notion, since g and h must lie in F[x]. Since degrees add (@thm-degree-of-product), a factorization p = gh with p 
eq 0 has \deg g + \deg h = \deg p. So g is constant exactly when \deg h = \deg p. This gives a working form of the definition: a non-constant p is reducible if and only if p = gh with 1 \le \deg g < \deg p and 1 \le \deg h < \deg p. [First Irreducible and Reducible Polynomials] 1. Show that every polynomial of degree 1 is irreducible over every field. 2. Show that the constants 0 and 2 are not irreducible over 
Q. 3. Show that x^2 + x is reducible over every field, and that x^3 is reducible over every field. (a) If \deg p = 1 and p = gh, then \deg g + \deg h = 1 with both degrees in 
N, so one of them is 0: one factor is a constant. Condition (1) holds since \deg p = 1. Hence p is irreducible, whatever the field. For example x, 2x + 4 and x - \sqrt2 (over 
R) are irreducible. (b) Both are constants, so condition (1) fails. They are the degenerate cases, and they matter: 2 divides everything in 
Q[x], like 1 among the integers, and it is not a building block. (c) x^2 + x = x(x + 1) with both factors of degree 1, and x^3 = x \cdot x^2 with factors of degrees 1 and 2. In each case both factors are non-constant, so condition (2) fails. Why insist on “non-constant”? For the same reason 1 is not a prime. If non-zero constants were allowed as building blocks, factorizations could never be unique: x = 2 \cdot 	frac12 x = 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 	frac16 x = \cdots over 
Q, with any number of constant factors. The factorization theorem below pulls out one constant in front and uses only non-constant, monic irreducibles. For polynomials of degree 2 and 3, irreducibility is decided by roots alone. [Irreducibility in Degree 2 and 3] Let F be a field and p \in F[x]. 1. p has a factor of degree 1 in F[x] if and only if p has a root in F. In particular, if \deg p \ge 2 and p has a root in F, then p is reducible over F. 2. If \deg p \in \{2, 3\}, then p is irreducible over F if and only if p has no root in F. (a) (⇐) If c \in F is a root, then p = (x - c)q by @thm-remainder-theorem (b). (⇒) If p = (ax + b)q with a 
eq 0, then c = -a^{-1} b satisfies ac + b = 0, so p(c) = 0 \cdot q(c) = 0 by @thm-evaluation-respects-operations. For the last sentence, if \deg p \ge 2 and p = (x - c)q, then \deg q = \deg p - 1 \ge 1, so both factors are non-constant of degree less than \deg p, and p is reducible. (b) We prove both directions by contraposition. (⇒) If p has a root, it is reducible by (a), since \deg p \ge 2. (⇐) Suppose p is reducible. By the working form of the definition, p = gh with \deg g, \deg h \ge 1 and \deg g + \deg h = \deg p \in \{2, 3\}. Two integers that are at least 1 and sum to 2 or 3 cannot both be at least 2, so one of g, h has degree 1. By (a), p has a root in F. This proves the theorem. For polynomials this follows quickly from the previous section. The first step is that an irreducible polynomial has only two possible gcds with anything. [The gcd with an Irreducible Polynomial] Let F be a field, p \in F[x] irreducible over F, and f \in F[x]. Then either p \mid f or \gcd(p, f) = 1. Let d = \gcd(p, f). Since p 
eq 0, d is monic, and d \mid p by @thm-gcd-properties (a), say p = du. Since p is irreducible, d or u is a constant. If d is a constant, then d = 1, since d is monic. If u is a constant, it is non-zero, and p = ud divides every multiple of d; since d \mid f by @thm-gcd-properties (a), @prp-divisibility-properties (a) gives p \mid f. This proves the lemma. [Euclid’s Lemma for Polynomials] Let F be a field and p \in F[x] irreducible over F. If q, r \in F[x] and p \mid qr, then p \mid q or p \mid r. Suppose p 
mid q. By @lem-irreducible-gcd, \gcd(p, q) = 1. Since p \mid qr, @thm-coprime-divides-product gives p \mid r. This proves the theorem. The hypothesis “irreducible” is essential. The polynomial x^2 divides x \cdot x but divides neither factor; the lemma does not apply because x^2 = x \cdot x is reducible. Over 
F_2, x^2 + 1 = (x + 1)^2 divides (x + 1)(x + 1) but not x + 1, for the same reason. For unique factorization we need the lemma for products of any length, and we need to know what “divides” means between two monic irreducibles. [Euclid’s Lemma for Several Factors] Let F be a field and p \in F[x] irreducible over F. 1. If q_1, \dots, q_k \in F[x] with k \ge 1 and p \mid q_1 q_2 \cdots q_k, then p \mid q_i for some i. 2. If q is irreducible over F, p \mid q, and p, q are both monic, then p = q. (a) We use induction on k. For k = 1 there is nothing to prove. Let k \ge 2 and assume the statement for k - 1 factors. Since p \mid (q_1 \cdots q_{k-1}) \, q_k, @thm-euclid-lemma-polynomials gives p \mid q_1 \cdots q_{k-1} or p \mid q_k. In the first case the induction hypothesis gives p \mid q_i for some i \le k - 1. Either way the statement holds for k. (b) Write q = pu. Since q is irreducible, p or u is constant. But p is not constant, being irreducible, so u is a non-zero constant. Comparing leading coefficients of the monic polynomials q and p gives u = 1, so p = q. Unique factorization Here is the theorem that Chapter 0’s remark about primes was pointing towards, now for polynomials. The constant in front is forced to be the leading coefficient; the rest is a product of monic irreducibles, unique up to order. [Unique Factorization in F\lbrack xbrack] Let F be a field and f \in F[x] non-constant. 1. Existence. There are a non-zero constant c \in F, an integer k \ge 1, and monic polynomials p_1, \dots, p_k \in F[x], each irreducible over F, with f = c \, p_1 p_2 \cdots p_k . 2. Uniqueness. If also f = c' \, q_1 q_2 \cdots q_l with c' \in F non-zero, l \ge 1, and q_1, \dots, q_l monic and irreducible over F, then c = c', k = l, and after renumbering the q_j we have p_i = q_i for every i. In both factorizations, the constant is the leading coefficient of f. Existence: if f is irreducible, stop; otherwise split it into two factors of smaller degree and factor each of them, which is strong induction on the degree. Uniqueness: compare leading coefficients to get c = c'. Then p_k divides q_1 \cdots q_l, so by Euclid’s lemma it equals some q_j. Cancel it from both sides; the two shorter factorizations are equal by induction on the number of factors k. The one thing to watch is that after canceling, the right-hand side must still have at least one factor. First a remark used in both parts. A product of monic polynomials is monic, by @thm-degree-of-product and induction on the number of factors. So if f = c \, p_1 \cdots p_k with the p_i monic, then the leading coefficient of f is c \cdot 1 = c. This proves the final sentence of the theorem. (a) We prove by strong induction on n \ge 1 (@thm-strong-induction with n_0 = 1) that every f of degree n has a factorization as in (a). Let \deg f = n, assume the statement for all degrees 1 \le m < n, and let c be the leading coefficient of f. Case 1: f is irreducible over F. Then f = c \, (c^{-1} f). The polynomial c^{-1} f is monic, and it is irreducible: it is non-constant, and if c^{-1} f = gh, then f = (cg)h, so cg or h is constant, hence g or h is constant. So k = 1, p_1 = c^{-1} f works. Case 2: f is reducible over F. By the working form of the definition, f = gh with 1 \le \deg g < n and 1 \le \deg h < n. By the induction hypothesis, g = a \, p_1 \cdots p_s and h = b \, p_{s+1} \cdots p_{s+t} with a, b non-zero constants, s, t \ge 1, and all p_i monic irreducible. Then f = (ab) \, p_1 \cdots p_{s+t}, with ab 
eq 0 by @thm-field-basic-properties. This is a factorization as in (a), with k = s + t. (b) By the first remark, c and c' are both the leading coefficient of f, so c = c'. Multiplying by c^{-1}, we get p_1 \cdots p_k = q_1 \cdots q_l. So it suffices to prove, by induction on k \ge 1, the statement U(k): whenever p_1 \cdots p_k = q_1 \cdots q_l with l \ge 1 and all p_i, q_j monic and irreducible over F, we have k = l, and after renumbering the q_j, p_i = q_i for every i. We first note: if a monic irreducible q equals a product r_1 \cdots r_m of m \ge 2 monic irreducibles, then q = r_1 \cdot (r_2 \cdots r_m) with both factors non-constant, since each r_i has degree at least 1; this contradicts the irreducibility of q. So a monic irreducible is never a product of two or more monic irreducibles. (\ast) Base case k = 1. Then p_1 = q_1 \cdots q_l. By (\ast), l = 1, and so p_1 = q_1. Inductive step. Let k \ge 2 and assume U(k - 1). Suppose p_1 \cdots p_k = q_1 \cdots q_l. If l = 1, then q_1 = p_1 \cdots p_k with k \ge 2, which is impossible by (\ast). So l \ge 2. Now p_k \mid q_1 \cdots q_l, so by @cor-euclid-lemma-products (a), p_k \mid q_j for some j, and by @cor-euclid-lemma-products (b), p_k = q_j. Renumber the q’s so that j = l. Then (p_1 \cdots p_{k-1}) \, p_k = (q_1 \cdots q_{l-1}) \, p_k , and since p_k 
eq 0, @cor-polynomial-no-zero-divisors (2) lets us cancel it: p_1 \cdots p_{k-1} = q_1 \cdots q_{l-1}, with k - 1 \ge 1 and l - 1 \ge 1 factors. By U(k - 1), k - 1 = l - 1, and after renumbering q_1, \dots, q_{l-1}, p_i = q_i for i \le k - 1. Together with p_k = q_k, this proves U(k). By induction, U(k) holds for every k \ge 1, which proves (b). Grouping equal factors, every non-constant f \in F[x] can be written uniquely as f = c \, p_1^{e_1} p_2^{e_2} \cdots p_s^{e_s} with c the leading coefficient, p_1, \dots, p_s distinct monic irreducibles over F, and exponents e_i \ge 1. Z[x] for the polynomials in 
Q[x] whose coefficients are all integers, as in the first section. Every rational number can be written as u/v with u \in 
Z, v \ge 1, and the only positive integer dividing both u and v equal to 1: take v \ge 1 as small as possible, since a common divisor e > 1 would give the representation (u/e)/(v/e) with a smaller denominator. We say u/v is in lowest terms. [Rational Root Theorem] Let f = a_n x^n + a_{n-1} x^{n-1} + \dots + a_0 \in 
Z[x] with n \ge 1 and a_n 
eq 0. If u/v \in 
Q is in lowest terms and f(u/v) = 0, then u \mid a_0 and v \mid a_n. Clear denominators: v^n f(u/v) = a_n u^n + a_{n-1} u^{n-1} v + \dots + a_0 v^n = 0. Every term except the last contains u, so u divides a_0 v^n; every term except the first contains v, so v divides a_n u^n. Since u and v share no factor, the powers of v can be stripped off one at a time, using Bézout for integers. Multiplying f(u/v) = 0 by v^n gives a_n u^n + a_{n-1} u^{n-1} v + \dots + a_1 u v^{n-1} + a_0 v^n = 0 . Since v \ge 1 and the only positive common divisor of u and v is 1, @lem-bezout-integers gives integers s, t with us + vt = 1. If b \in 
Z and k \ge 1 with u \mid b v^k, then b v^{k-1} = b v^{k-1}(us + vt) = u \, (b v^{k-1} s) + t \, (b v^k) is a sum of two multiples of u, so u \mid b v^{k-1}. Applying this n times to b = a_0 gives u \mid a_0. Similarly, if v \mid c u^k with k \ge 1, then c u^{k-1} = s \, (c u^k) + v \, (c u^{k-1} t), so v \mid c u^{k-1}; applying this n times to c = a_n gives v \mid a_n. This proves the theorem.
