Expanding along the first row, \det L_0 = \det egin{pmatrix} 3 & -1 & -1 \ -1 & 2 & -1 \ -1 & -1 & 3 \end{pmatrix} = 3(6 - 1) + 1\cdot(-3 - 1) - 1\cdot(1 + 2) = 15 - 4 - 3 = 8 . (b) There are  inom{5}{3} = 10 sets of three edges. Three edges on four vertices connect everything exactly when they contain no cycle, and the only 3-edge cycles are the triangles \{e_1, e_2, e_5\} (vertices 1, 2, 3) and \{e_3, e_4, e_5\} (vertices 1, 3, 4). So there are 10 - 2 = 8 spanning trees, matching \det L_0. (c) Deleting row 4 of N deletes row 4 of NN	p (row view) and column 4 of NN	p (column view of N	p), by @thm-three-views-of-product. So L_0 = N_0N_0	p, with N_0 \in M_{3 	imes 5}(
R), and @cor-gram-determinant-nonnegative gives \det L_0 = \sum_{|S| = 3} (\det (N_0)_{[3],S})^2, one term for each set S of three edges. (d) For S = \{e_1, e_2, e_3\}, (N_0)_{[3],S} =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \ -1 & 1 & 0 \ 0 & -1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, which is lower triangular with determinant 1 (@thm-det-triangular). For S = \{e_1, e_2, e_5\}, the columns are (1, -1, 0), (0, 1, -1), (1, 0, -1), and the third is the sum of the first two: going around the cycle 1 	o 2 	o 3 equals going directly 1 	o 3. So the columns are dependent and the minor is 0 by @thm-alternating-properties. Thus the non-tree contributes 0^2 and the tree contributes 1^2. [C2: Rank does not depend on the field] Let K be a subfield of a field L (@def-restriction-of-scalars), and let A \in M_{m 	imes n}(K). We may also regard A as a matrix in M_{m 	imes n}(L). 1. Explain why each minor \det A_{I,J} is the same element whether computed in K or in L. 2. Prove that the rank of A over K equals its rank over L. 3. Deduce: if a system A\x = \0 with rational coefficients has a non-zero complex solution, it has a non-zero rational solution. (a) By @def-determinant, \det A_{I,J} is a finite sum of \pm products of entries of A. The entries lie in K, and K has the same addition and multiplication as L, so the sum is the same element of K \subseteq L. (b) If A = 0, both ranks are 0. Otherwise, by @thm-rank-via-minors (a) applied over K and over L, each rank is the largest k for which some k 	imes k minor is non-zero. By (a) the list of minors, and which of them are non-zero, is the same in both cases. Hence the two ranks agree. (c) Take K = 
Q, L = 
C. A non-zero complex solution means 
ullity A \ge 1 over 
C, so ank_{
C} A \le n - 1 by @thm-rank-nullity-matrix. By (b), ank_{
Q} A \le n - 1, so 
ullity A \ge 1 over 
Q, and a non-zero rational solution exists.

title: 6.8 Special Determinants
content:
Special Determinants A determinant of size n has n! terms, so a general formula for a large matrix is hopeless. Some matrices, though, have so much structure that their determinants collapse to a short product or a recurrence. This section computes the most useful of them: the Vandermonde determinant, which governs polynomial interpolation; tridiagonal determinants, which satisfy a three-term recurrence; block triangular determinants, which split into smaller ones; and the determinant of a rank-one update of the identity. The proofs share one idea: find the structure first (a polynomial with known roots, a row with two non-zero entries, a pattern of zeros) and let the defining properties of the determinant do the rest. The Vandermonde determinant Chapter 2 proved that there is exactly one polynomial of degree at most n through n + 1 points with distinct first coordinates (@thm-interpolation-unique). Behind it sat a square matrix of powers of the nodes. Its determinant turns out to be a product of all the differences of the nodes, and that product explains at a glance why distinct nodes are exactly what is needed. For x_1, \dots, x_n \in F, the Vandermonde matrix is V(x_1, \dots, x_n) \coloneqq  egin{pmatrix} 1 & x_1 & x_1^2 & \cdots & x_1^{n-1} \ 1 & x_2 & x_2^2 & \cdots & x_2^{n-1} \ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & & \vdots \ 1 & x_n & x_n^2 & \cdots & x_n^{n-1} \end{pmatrix} \in M_n(F), whose (i, j)-entry is x_i^{j-1}. Row i lists the powers 1, x_i, \dots, x_i^{n-1} of the i-th node. For n = 1 it is the 1 	imes 1 matrix (1), and for n = 2 its determinant is x_2 - x_1. [Vandermonde Determinant] Let n \ge 1 and x_1, \dots, x_n \in F. Then \det V(x_1, \dots, x_n) = \prod_{1 \le i < j \le n} (x_j - x_i), where the empty product (for n = 1) is 1. Induction on n. Replace the last node x_n by a variable t. Expanding along the last row shows the determinant is a polynomial f(t) of degree at most n - 1, with leading coefficient the smaller Vandermonde determinant. Setting t = x_i for i < n makes two rows equal, so x_1, \dots, x_{n-1} are roots of f. A polynomial of degree at most n - 1 with these n - 1 roots is its leading coefficient times \prod_{i<n}(t - x_i). Now put t = x_n back. The roots argument needs the x_i distinct; if they are not, both sides are 0 anyway. We use induction on n (@thm-induction). For n = 1, \det(1) = 1, the empty product. Let n \ge 2, assume the formula for n - 1 nodes, and write V = V(x_1, \dots, x_n). Let C_{n1}, \dots, C_{nn} be the cofactors of V along row n (@def-minor-cofactor). Each C_{nj} is computed after deleting row n, so it does not involve x_n. Define f(t) \coloneqq \sum_{j=1}^{n} C_{nj}\, t^{j-1} \in F[t] . For c \in F, let V_c be V with row n replaced by (1, c, \dots, c^{n-1}). Then V_c has the same cofactors along row n as V, so by @thm-laplace-expansion along row n, \det V_c = \sum_{j=1}^{n} c^{j-1} C_{nj} = f(c) . 	ag{$\ast$} In particular \det V = f(x_n). The coefficient of t^{n-1} in f is C_{nn} = (-1)^{2n}\det V(x_1, \dots, x_{n-1}), since deleting row n and column n of V leaves the Vandermonde matrix of the first n - 1 nodes. Case 1: two of x_1, \dots, x_{n-1} are equal, say x_p = x_q with p < q < n. Then rows p and q of V are equal. By @thm-det-transpose, \det V = \det V	p, and V	p has two equal columns, so \det V = 0 because the determinant is alternating (@def-alternating-form). The product also vanishes, since it contains the factor x_q - x_p = 0. Case 2: x_1, \dots, x_{n-1} are distinct. For i < n, the matrix V_{x_i} has rows i and n equal, so f(x_i) = \det V_{x_i} = 0 by (\ast) and the argument of Case 1. Hence x_1, \dots, x_{n-1} are n - 1 distinct roots of f, and by @cor-root-bound-general, g(t) \coloneqq (t - x_1)(t - x_2)\cdots(t - x_{n-1}) \ 	ext{ divides } \ f . Write f = hg with h \in F[t]. If h 
e 0, then \deg h = \deg f - (n - 1) \le 0 by @thm-degree-of-product, since \deg f \le n - 1; so in every case h is a constant h \in F. As g is monic of degree n - 1, the coefficient of t^{n-1} in hg is h, so h = C_{nn} = \det V(x_1, \dots, x_{n-1}). Evaluating at x_n (@thm-evaluation-respects-operations) and using the induction hypothesis, \det V = f(x_n) = \det V(x_1, \dots, x_{n-1}) \prod_{i=1}^{n-1}(x_n - x_i) = \prod_{1 \le i < j \le n-1}(x_j - x_i) \prod_{i=1}^{n-1}(x_n - x_i) . The two products together run over all pairs i < j \le n, the second one collecting exactly the pairs with j = n. This proves the formula for n, and the theorem follows by induction. [A 3 	imes 3 Vandermonde Determinant] Compute \det V(1, 2, 4) from the formula and by cofactor expansion. The formula gives (2 - 1)(4 - 1)(4 - 2) = 1 \cdot 3 \cdot 2 = 6. Directly, expanding V(1, 2, 4) =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \ 1 & 2 & 4 \ 1 & 4 & 16 \end{pmatrix} along the first row gives 1\cdot(32 - 16) - 1\cdot(16 - 4) + 1\cdot(4 - 2) = 16 - 12 + 2 = 6. The product vanishes exactly when a factor does, because a field has no zero divisors. So: [Distinct Nodes Give an Invertible Vandermonde Matrix] V(x_1, \dots, x_n) is invertible if and only if x_1, \dots, x_n are distinct. In a field, a product is non-zero if and only if every factor is non-zero (@thm-field-basic-properties (f), applied repeatedly). So by @thm-vandermonde-determinant, \det V(x_1, \dots, x_n) 
e 0 if and only if x_j 
e x_i for all i < j. By @thm-det-nonzero-iff-invertible, this is equivalent to invertibility. Now the promised two-line proof of @thm-interpolation-unique. Given distinct x_0, \dots, x_n and values y_0, \dots, y_n, a polynomial p = c_0 + c_1x + \dots + c_nx^n satisfies p(x_i) = y_i for all i if and only if V(x_0, \dots, x_n)\,\c = \y, since row i of this system reads c_0 + c_1x_i + \dots + c_nx_i^n = y_i. By @cor-vandermonde-nonzero the matrix is invertible, so the system has exactly one solution \c = V(x_0, \dots, x_n)^{-1}\y (@thm-invertible-tfae), and the interpolating polynomial exists and is unique. This is not a proof from nothing. The root bound of Chapter 5 did the real work inside @thm-vandermonde-determinant, exactly as the root bound did in Chapter 2. What the determinant adds is an explicit number: it says how close to singular the interpolation problem is, since nodes that nearly coincide make the product small. Watch the shape and the order. The formula is for rows (1, x_i, \dots, x_i^{n-1}) starting at the power 0, and for the factors x_j - x_i with i < j, “later node minus earlier node”. Dropping the column of ones changes the answer: \det egin{pmatrix} x_1 & x_1^2 \ x_2 & x_2^2 \end{pmatrix} = x_1x_2(x_2 - x_1), not x_2 - x_1. Writing the factors as x_i - x_j instead flips the sign of each of the  inom{n}{2} factors, so it multiplies the answer by (-1)^{ inom{n}{2}}: already for n = 2 and n = 3 this is -1, a wrong sign. Without expanding, find \det V(1, 2, 3, 5). The pairs i < j give (2 - 1)(3 - 1)(5 - 1)(3 - 2)(5 - 2)(5 - 3) = 1 \cdot 2 \cdot 4 \cdot 1 \cdot 3 \cdot 2 = 48. Tridiagonal determinants Many matrices in applications have non-zero entries only on the diagonal and next to it: discretized differential equations, chains of springs, the recurrences of orthogonal polynomials. Such a matrix is tridiagonal. Its determinant is not a closed formula in general, but it obeys a recurrence in the size, because the last row has only two non-zero entries. Let T_n \in M_n(F) have diagonal entries a_1, \dots, a_n, entries b_1, \dots, b_{n-1} just above the diagonal ((i, i+1)-entry b_i), entries c_1, \dots, c_{n-1} just below it ((i+1, i)-entry c_i), and zeros elsewhere: T_n =  egin{pmatrix} a_1 & b_1 & & & \ c_1 & a_2 & b_2 & & \ & c_2 & \ddots & \ddots & \ & & \ddots & a_{n-1} & b_{n-1} \ & & & c_{n-1} & a_n \end{pmatrix}. For 1 \le k \le n, the top-left k 	imes k block of T_n is the tridiagonal matrix T_k built from a_1, \dots, a_k, b_1, \dots, b_{k-1}, c_1, \dots, c_{k-1}. Write D_k = \det T_k, and set D_0 = 1. [Tridiagonal Recurrence] With this notation, D_1 = a_1, and for 2 \le k \le n, D_k = a_k\,D_{k-1} - b_{k-1}c_{k-1}\,D_{k-2} . D_1 = \det(a_1) = a_1. For k = 2, D_2 = a_1a_2 - b_1c_1 = a_2D_1 - b_1c_1D_0. Let k \ge 3. Row k of T_k has only two possibly non-zero entries, c_{k-1} in column k - 1 and a_k in column k. By @thm-laplace-expansion along row k, D_k = c_{k-1}(-1)^{2k-1}M_{k,k-1} + a_k(-1)^{2k}M_{kk} = a_kM_{kk} - c_{k-1}M_{k,k-1}, where M_{kk} = \det T_{k-1} = D_{k-1}. The minor M_{k,k-1} is the determinant of the (k - 1) 	imes (k - 1) matrix obtained by deleting row k and column k - 1. Its last column consists of rows 1, \dots, k - 1 of column k of T_k, which is b_{k-1} in the last position and 0 elsewhere. Expanding along this last column (@thm-laplace-expansion), with sign (-1)^{(k-1)+(k-1)} = 1, gives M_{k,k-1} = b_{k-1}\det T_{k-2} = b_{k-1}D_{k-2}, because deleting the last row and column leaves rows and columns 1, \dots, k - 2 of T_k. Substituting proves the recurrence. [Fibonacci Numbers as Determinants] Let T_n have 1 on the diagonal, 1 above it and -1 below it. Find D_n = \det T_n. Here a_k = 1 and b_{k-1}c_{k-1} = 1 \cdot (-1) = -1, so @thm-tridiagonal-recurrence gives D_k = D_{k-1} + D_{k-2} for k \ge 2, with D_0 = 1 and D_1 = 1. Hence D_1, D_2, D_3, \dots = 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, 34, \dots, the Fibonacci numbers: D_n = F_{n+1}, where F_1 = F_2 = 1 and F_{k} = F_{k-1} + F_{k-2}. For instance D_3 = \det egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 0 \ -1 & 1 & 1 \ 0 & -1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = 1\cdot(1 + 1) - 1\cdot(-1 - 0) + 0 = 3 . Only the products b_{k-1}c_{k-1} enter the recurrence, never b_{k-1} and c_{k-1} separately. For example, for a real number t, putting 2t on the diagonal and 1 on both neighboring lines gives D_k = 2t\,D_{k-1} - D_{k-2}, so D_1 = 2t, D_2 = 4t^2 - 1, D_3 = 8t^3 - 4t. These are the Chebyshev polynomials of the second kind. Block triangular matrices A matrix can be cut into blocks by a horizontal and a vertical line. When the block in the lower left is zero, the determinant should see only the two square blocks on the diagonal, just as a triangular determinant sees only diagonal entries. This result is used constantly, for instance in Chapter 7 for Schur complements. [Block Triangular Determinant] Let A \in M_k(F), D \in M_l(F) and B \in M_{k 	imes l}(F), with k, l \ge 1. Then \det egin{pmatrix} A & B \ 0 & D \end{pmatrix} = \det A \cdot \det D , where 0 is the l 	imes k zero matrix. The same holds for  egin{pmatrix} A & 0 \ C & D \end{pmatrix} with C \in M_{l 	imes k}(F). In the Leibniz formula for the whole matrix, a term picks one entry from each column. The first k columns have zeros below row k, so a non-zero term must pick rows 1, \dots, k for the first k columns, and is then forced to pick rows k+1, \dots, n for the last l columns. Such a permutation is a permutation of each block, its inversions are the inversions inside the blocks, and the Leibniz sum factors into two Leibniz sums. Let n = k + l and M =  egin{pmatrix} A & B \ 0 & D \end{pmatrix} = (m_{ij}). By @def-determinant, \det M = \sum_{\sigma \in S_n} \sgn(\sigma) \prod_{j=1}^{n} m_{\sigma(j)j}. Since m_{ij} = 0 for i > k \ge j, the term of \sigma is 0 unless \sigma(j) \le k for every j \le k. For such \sigma, the injective map \sigma sends \{1, \dots, k\} into itself, hence onto itself (a finite set), and so it sends \{k+1, \dots, n\} onto itself. Therefore \sigma determines \alpha \in S_k and  eta \in S_l by \alpha(j) = \sigma(j) \quad (j \le k), \qquad  eta(q) = \sigma(k + q) - k \quad (q \le l), and every pair (\alpha,  eta) arises from exactly one such \sigma. We compare signs through inversions (@def-inversion). A pair i < j with i, j \le k is an inversion of \sigma exactly when it is one of \alpha; a pair k + p < k + q is an inversion of \sigma exactly when p < q is one of  eta; and a pair i \le k < j is never an inversion, since \sigma(i) \le k < \sigma(j). By @def-sign-permutation, \sgn(\sigma) = \sgn(\alpha)\sgn( eta). Also m_{\sigma(j)j} = a_{\alpha(j)j} for j \le k and m_{\sigma(k+q),k+q} = d_{ eta(q)q}. Hence \det M = \sum_{\alpha \in S_k}\sum_{ eta \in S_l} \sgn(\alpha)\sgn( eta) \prod_{j=1}^{k} a_{\alpha(j)j} \prod_{q=1}^{l} d_{ eta(q)q} = \det A \cdot \det D, using @def-determinant twice. For the lower block triangular case, the transpose of  egin{pmatrix} A & 0 \ C & D \end{pmatrix} is  egin{pmatrix} A	p & C	p \ 0 & D	p \end{pmatrix}, so by @thm-det-transpose and the first case its determinant is \det A	p \det D	p = \det A \det D. The proof uses only sums and products of entries, so, like the results flagged in §4–§6, it holds for matrices over any commutative ring; §10 uses this over F[x]. By induction on the number of blocks, a matrix with square blocks A_1, \dots, A_r on the diagonal and zeros below them has determinant \det A_1 \cdots \det A_r; @thm-det-triangular is the case where every block is 1 	imes 1. For example, \det egin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & 5 & -3 \ 1 & 1 & 0 & 7 \ 0 & 0 & 3 & 1 \ 0 & 0 & 4 & 2 \end{pmatrix} = \det egin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\det egin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 \ 4 & 2 \end{pmatrix} = 1 \cdot 2 = 2, and the entries 5, -3, 0, 7 of the upper right block play no role. There is no “block ad - bc” rule. For a general block matrix, \det egin{pmatrix} A & B \ C & D \end{pmatrix} 
e \det A\det D - \det B\det C. Take A = D = 0 and B = C = I_2: the 4 	imes 4 matrix  egin{pmatrix} 0 & I_2 \ I_2 & 0 \end{pmatrix} is the permutation matrix of (1\ 3)(2\ 4), a product of two transpositions, so its determinant is +1; the rule would give 0 \cdot 0 - 1 \cdot 1 = -1. The zero block in the corner is what the theorem needs. The correct formulas for general blocks use Schur complements, in Chapter 7. Is \det egin{pmatrix} A & B \ 0 & D \end{pmatrix} = \det A \det D meaningful when A is 2 	imes 3 and D is 3 	imes 2 (so the whole matrix is 5 	imes 5)? No. The theorem requires A and D square; here \det A and \det D are undefined. In fact the whole determinant is 0 whatever the entries: the first 3 columns have their non-zero entries only in the first 2 rows, so they are linearly dependent in a 2-dimensional space, and a determinant with dependent columns is 0 (@thm-alternating-properties). Rank-one updates Changing a matrix by a rank-one matrix \u\v	p is the smallest possible change in the sense of rank, and it happens often: updating one observation in statistics, modifying one row of a system, or adding the same number to every entry. The determinant of the updated identity turns out to be a single dot product. [Matrix Determinant Lemma] Let \u, \v \in F^n. Then \det(I_n + \u\v	p) = 1 + \v	p\u . Border I_n + \u\v	p by an extra column \u and an extra row (\0	p, 1), giving a block triangular matrix M with the same determinant. Then clear the update by elimination with blocks. Rows: add \v	p times the top n rows to the new bottom row (multiply by L on the left). Columns: subtract the last column times \v	p from the first n columns (multiply by L' on the right). The factors L, L' have determinant 1, and the result is block triangular with I_n and the 1 	imes 1 block 1 + \v	p\u on the diagonal. Consider the (n+1) 	imes (n+1) block matrices L =  egin{pmatrix} I_n & \0 \ \v	p & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad M =  egin{pmatrix} I_n + \u\v	p & \u \ \0	p & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad L' =  egin{pmatrix} I_n & \0 \ -\v	p & 1 \end{pmatrix}. Splitting the sum \sum_{j} in @thm-three-views-of-product (1) into the indices j \le n and j = n + 1 shows that matrices partitioned in this way multiply block by block, like 2 	imes 2 matrices whose entries are blocks. Hence LM =  egin{pmatrix} I_n + \u\v	p & \u \ \v	p + (\v	p\u)\v	p & \v	p\u + 1 \end{pmatrix}, where we used \v	p(\u\v	p) = (\v	p\u)\v	p by associativity, \v	p\u being a 1 	imes 1 matrix, that is, a scalar. Multiplying on the right by L', LML' =  egin{pmatrix} I_n + \u\v	p - \u\v	p & \u \ \v	p + (\v	p\u)\v	p - (1 + \v	p\u)\v	p & 1 + \v	p\u \end{pmatrix} =  egin{pmatrix} I_n & \u \ \0	p & 1 + \v	p\u \end{pmatrix}. By @thm-det-block-triangular, \det L = \det I_n \cdot 1 = 1, \det L' = 1, \det M = \det(I_n + \u\v	p) \cdot 1, and \det(LML') = \det I_n\,(1 + \v	p\u) = 1 + \v	p\u. By @thm-det-multiplicative, \det(LML') = \det L\det M\det L' = \det(I_n + \u\v	p). This proves the lemma. [a on the Diagonal, 1 Elsewhere] Let a \in 
R and n \ge 1, and let A_n \in M_n(
R) have every diagonal entry a and every other entry 1. Find \det A_n. Let \mathbf{1} = (1, \dots, 1) \in 
R^n. Every entry of \mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}	p is 1, so A_n = (a - 1)I_n + \mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}	p. Case a 
e 1. Then A_n = (a - 1) ig(I_n + \u\mathbf{1}	p ig) with \u =  rac{1}{a-1}\mathbf{1}. Scaling an n 	imes n matrix by c multiplies its determinant by c^n (multilinearity in each of the n columns), so by @thm-matrix-determinant-lemma \det A_n = (a - 1)^n\Big(1 +  rac{n}{a - 1}\Big) = (a - 1)^{n-1}(a - 1 + n), since \mathbf{1}	p\u =  rac{n}{a-1}. Case a = 1. For n \ge 2, all columns are equal, so \det A_n = 0, which the formula also gives. For n = 1, \det A_1 = 1, and the formula gives (a - 1)^0 \cdot 1 = 1. So \det A_n = (a - 1)^{n-1}(a + n - 1) for every a. For n = 3 this is (a - 1)^2(a + 2); with a = 3 it gives 4 \cdot 5 = 20. The lemma is about I_n + \u\v	p, not \u\v	p or \u	p\v. The rank-one matrix \u\v	p is n 	imes n and, for n \ge 2, has determinant 0; the scalar \v	p\u is its trace. Do not confuse \det(I_n + \u\v	p) = 1 + \v	p\u with \det(I_n) + \det(\u\v	p) = 1 (for n \ge 2), which is false whenever \v	p\u 
e 0: for \u = \v = \e_1, I_n + \e_1\e_1	p = \diag(2, 1, \dots, 1) has determinant 2. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. State the Vandermonde determinant formula, including the order of the factors. 2. True or false: V(x_1, \dots, x_n) is invertible whenever x_1, \dots, x_n are non-zero. Justify your answer. 3. Write down the recurrence for the determinant of a tridiagonal matrix, and say which row the proof expands along. 4. True or false: \det egin{pmatrix} A & B \ C & D \end{pmatrix} = \det A\det D whenever A and D are square and B = 0. Justify your answer. 5. True or false: \det(I_n + \u\v	p) = \det(I_n + \v\u	p) for all \u, \v \in F^n. Justify your answer. (a) \det V(x_1, \dots, x_n) = \prod_{1 \le i < j \le n}(x_j - x_i), where V has (i, j)-entry x_i^{j-1} (@thm-vandermonde-determinant). (b) False. V(1, 1) =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} has non-zero nodes and determinant 0. The condition is that the nodes are distinct (@cor-vandermonde-nonzero); 0 is allowed as a node. (c) D_k = a_kD_{k-1} - b_{k-1}c_{k-1}D_{k-2}, with D_0 = 1, D_1 = a_1 (@thm-tridiagonal-recurrence). The proof expands along the last row, which has only two non-zero entries. (d) True. With B = 0 the matrix is lower block triangular, and @thm-det-block-triangular applies. (e) True. Both equal 1 + \v	p\u = 1 + \u	p\v by @thm-matrix-determinant-lemma, since \v	p\u = \sum_i v_iu_i = \u	p\v. B. Practice [B1: A 4 	imes 4 Vandermonde determinant] Compute \det egin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 & 1 & -1 \ 1 & 0 & 0 & 0 \ 1 & 1 & 1 & 1 \ 1 & 2 & 4 & 8 \end{pmatrix}. Hence decide whether there is exactly one polynomial p \in 
R[x]_{\le 3} with p(-1) = 3, p(0) = 1, p(1) = 0, p(2) = 5. Row i is (1, x_i, x_i^2, x_i^3) with nodes -1, 0, 1, 2, so this is V(-1, 0, 1, 2). By @thm-vandermonde-determinant its determinant is (0 - (-1))(1 - (-1))(2 - (-1))(1 - 0)(2 - 0)(2 - 1) = 1 \cdot 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 1 \cdot 2 \cdot 1 = 12 . (Check by expanding along row 2, which is (1, 0, 0, 0): the determinant is (-1)^{2+1}\det egin{pmatrix} -1 & 1 & -1 \ 1 & 1 & 1 \ 2 & 4 & 8 \end{pmatrix} = - ig({-1}(8 - 4) - 1(8 - 2) - 1(4 - 2) ig) = -(-4 - 6 - 2) = 12.) Hence the coefficient matrix of the interpolation system is invertible, and there is exactly one p \in 
R[x]_{\le 3} with the given values. [B2: The second-difference matrix] Let K_n \in M_n(
R) have 2 on the diagonal, -1 directly above and below it, and 0 elsewhere. Prove that \det K_n = n + 1. Hence show that K_n is invertible for every n. Here a_k = 2 and b_{k-1}c_{k-1} = (-1)(-1) = 1. By @thm-tridiagonal-recurrence, D_k = 2D_{k-1} - D_{k-2} for k \ge 2, with D_0 = 1, D_1 = 2. We show D_k = k + 1 by strong induction on k (@thm-strong-induction). It holds for k = 0, 1. If it holds for k - 1 and k - 2, then D_k = 2k - (k - 1) = k + 1. Hence \det K_n = D_n = n + 1 
e 0, and K_n is invertible by @thm-det-nonzero-iff-invertible. [B3: A rank-one update] Let \u = (1, 2, 3) and \v = (1, -1, 2) in 
Q^3. 1. Use @thm-matrix-determinant-lemma to find \det(I_3 + \u\v	p). 2. Write out I_3 + \u\v	p and check your answer by elimination. 3. Find all t \in 
Q for which I_3 + t\,\u\v	p is not invertible. (a) \v	p\u = 1 - 2 + 6 = 5, so \det(I_3 + \u\v	p) = 6. (b) \u\v	p =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 & 2 \ 2 & -2 & 4 \ 3 & -3 & 6 \end{pmatrix}, so I_3 + \u\v	p =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 & 2 \ 2 & -1 & 4 \ 3 & -3 & 7 \end{pmatrix}. Subtract row 1 from row 2, which does not change the determinant (@thm-det-row-operations), to get row 2 equal to (0, 0, 2). Expanding along that row, \det = 2 \cdot (-1)^{2+3}\det egin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 \ 3 & -3 \end{pmatrix} = -2(-6 + 3) = 6 . (c) I_3 + t\,\u\v	p = I_3 + (t\u)\v	p, whose determinant is 1 + t\,\v	p\u = 1 + 5t. It is zero exactly for t = - rac15, and by @thm-det-nonzero-iff-invertible that is the only t for which the matrix is not invertible. C. Going deeper [C1: The Cauchy determinant] Let x_1, \dots, x_n, y_1, \dots, y_n \in F with x_i + y_j 
e 0 for all i, j, and let Q_n \in M_n(F) have (i, j)-entry \dfrac{1}{x_i + y_j}. The goal is \det Q_n =  rac{\prod_{1 \le i < j \le n}(x_j - x_i)(y_j - y_i)}{\prod_{i=1}^{n}\prod_{j=1}^{n}(x_i + y_j)} . 1. For i < n, subtract row n from row i. Show that the new (i, j)-entry is \dfrac{x_n - x_i}{(x_i + y_j)(x_n + y_j)}, and deduce that \det Q_n = \dfrac{\prod_{i<n}(x_n - x_i)}{\prod_{j}(x_n + y_j)}\det Q', where Q' agrees with Q_n in rows 1, \dots, n-1 and has last row (1, \dots, 1). 2. In Q', for j < n, subtract column n from column j. Deduce that \det Q' = \dfrac{\prod_{j<n}(y_n - y_j)}{\prod_{i<n}(x_i + y_n)}\det Q_{n-1}, where Q_{n-1} is built from x_1, \dots, x_{n-1} and y_1, \dots, y_{n-1}. 3. Prove the formula by induction on n. 4. The Hilbert matrix H_n has (i, j)-entry  rac{1}{i + j - 1}. Show that it is a Cauchy matrix, and use (c) to compute \det H_3. Hint: in (a) and (b), factor scalars out of whole rows and columns using multilinearity. (a) For i < n,  rac{1}{x_i + y_j} -  rac{1}{x_n + y_j} =  rac{(x_n + y_j) - (x_i + y_j)}{(x_i + y_j)(x_n + y_j)} =  rac{x_n - x_i}{(x_i + y_j)(x_n + y_j)}. These row operations do not change the determinant (@thm-det-row-operations). In the new matrix, row i < n has the factor x_n - x_i in every entry, and column j has the factor  rac{1}{x_n + y_j} in every entry (in row n,  rac{1}{x_n + y_j} =  rac{1}{x_n + y_j} \cdot 1). Pulling these scalars out of each row and column by multilinearity (@thm-det-row-operations, in its row and column forms) leaves the matrix Q' with entries  rac{1}{x_i + y_j} in rows i < n and 1 in row n. This gives the stated formula. (b) For j < n, subtracting column n from column j leaves the determinant unchanged, makes the last row (0, \dots, 0, 1), and for i < n gives  rac{1}{x_i + y_j} -  rac{1}{x_i + y_n} =  rac{y_n - y_j}{(x_i + y_j)(x_i + y_n)}. Pull y_n - y_j out of column j (j < n) and  rac{1}{x_i + y_n} out of row i (i < n); the last row (0, \dots, 0, 1) is unaffected by the column factors because its first n - 1 entries are 0, and row factors do not touch row n. What remains has  rac{1}{x_i + y_j} in positions i, j < n, entries (x_i + y_n)\cdot rac{1}{x_i + y_n} = 1 in column n above the corner, and last row (0, \dots, 0, 1). Expanding along the last row (@thm-laplace-expansion) gives \det Q_{n-1}, with sign (-1)^{2n} = 1. (c) For n = 1, \det Q_1 =  rac{1}{x_1 + y_1}, which is the formula with empty products upstairs. For n \ge 2, combining (a) and (b), \det Q_n =  rac{\prod_{i<n}(x_n - x_i)(y_n - y_i)}{\prod_{j \le n}(x_n + y_j)\prod_{i<n}(x_i + y_n)}\det Q_{n-1} . The numerator supplies exactly the factors of \prod_{i<j}(x_j - x_i)(y_j - y_i) with j = n, and the denominator supplies exactly the factors x_i + y_j with \max(i, j) = n, each once. By the induction hypothesis, \det Q_{n-1} supplies all the remaining factors. This proves the formula. (d) With x_i = i and y_j = j - 1, x_i + y_j = i + j - 1 \ge 1, so H_n is a Cauchy matrix over 
Q. For n = 3, the numerator is  ig((2-1)(3-1)(3-2) ig)^2 = 4, since y_j - y_i = j - i = x_j - x_i. The denominator is the product of all i + j - 1: the rows give 1 \cdot 2 \cdot 3 = 6, 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 4 = 24, 3 \cdot 4 \cdot 5 = 60, in total 8640. Hence \det H_3 =  rac{4}{8640} =  rac{1}{2160}. (In general \det H_n = c_n^4 / c_{2n} with c_n = \prod_{k=1}^{n-1} k!; we state this without proof. These determinants shrink extremely fast, which is why Hilbert matrices are a standard test of numerical methods.) [C2: A circulant determinant over 
C] Let a, b, c \in 
C, let \omega = e^{2\pi i/3}, and let Z =  egin{pmatrix} a & b & c \ c & a & b \ b & c & a \end{pmatrix}. 1. For k = 0, 1, 2, let \w_k = (1, \omega^k, \omega^{2k}) and \lambda_k = a + b\omega^k + c\omega^{2k}. Show that Z\w_k = \lambda_k\w_k. 2. Let W be the matrix with columns \w_0, \w_1, \w_2. Show that ZW = W\diag(\lambda_0, \lambda_1, \lambda_2) and that \det W 
e 0. Deduce \det Z = \lambda_0\lambda_1\lambda_2. 3. Using \omega^3 = 1 and 1 + \omega + \omega^2 = 0, deduce \det Z = a^3 + b^3 + c^3 - 3abc, and check this against the Leibniz formula. Circulant matrices of every size are treated in Chapter 11. (a) By @exm-roots-of-unity, \omega^3 = 1, so \omega^{-k} = \omega^{2k} and \omega^{-2k} = \omega^{k}. Row 1 of Z\w_k is a + b\omega^k + c\omega^{2k} = \lambda_k. Row 2 is c + a\omega^k + b\omega^{2k} = \omega^k(c\omega^{-k} + a + b\omega^k) = \omega^k(a + b\omega^k + c\omega^{2k}) = \omega^k\lambda_k. Row 3 is b + c\omega^k + a\omega^{2k} = \omega^{2k}(b\omega^{-2k} + c\omega^{-k} + a) = \omega^{2k}\lambda_k. Hence Z\w_k = \lambda_k\w_k. (b) By @thm-three-views-of-product, column k of ZW is Z\w_k = \lambda_k\w_k, which is column k of W\diag(\lambda_0, \lambda_1, \lambda_2). The (i, k)-entry of W is (\omega^k)^{i-1}, so W = V(1, \omega, \omega^2)	p. The nodes 1, \omega, \omega^2 are distinct (they are e^{2\pi ik/3} for k = 0, 1, 2), so \det W = \det V(1, \omega, \omega^2) 
e 0 by @thm-det-transpose and @cor-vandermonde-nonzero. By @thm-det-multiplicative and @thm-det-triangular, \det Z\det W = \det W\,\lambda_0\lambda_1\lambda_2, and canceling \det W 
e 0 gives \det Z = \lambda_0\lambda_1\lambda_2. (c) Multiply out \lambda_1\lambda_2 = (a + b\omega + c\omega^2)(a + b\omega^2 + c\omega). The nine terms are a^2, ab\omega^2 + ab\omega, ac\omega + ac\omega^2, b^2\omega^3, bc\omega^2, bc\omega^4 = bc\omega, c^2\omega^3. Using \omega^3 = 1 and \omega + \omega^2 = -1, \lambda_1\lambda_2 = a^2 + b^2 + c^2 - ab - ac - bc . Then \det Z = (a + b + c)(a^2 + b^2 + c^2 - ab - ac - bc) = a^3 + b^3 + c^3 - 3abc, expanding and canceling. The Leibniz formula for Z gives the three even terms a \cdot a \cdot a, c \cdot c \cdot c (from \sigma = (1\ 2\ 3)) and b \cdot b \cdot b, and the three odd terms, each equal to abc with sign -: the same answer. [C3: Rank-one updates of an invertible matrix] Let A \in M_n(F) be invertible and \u, \v \in F^n. 1. Prove that \det(A + \u\v	p) = \det A\, ig(1 + \v	p A^{-1}\u ig). 2. Deduce that A + \u\v	p is invertible if and only if \v	p A^{-1}\u 
e -1. 3. Give an example over 
Q with n = 2 where A is invertible, \u\v	p 
e 0, and A + \u\v	p is not invertible. (a) Since A is invertible, A + \u\v	p = A(I_n + A^{-1}\u\v	p) = A ig(I_n + (A^{-1}\u)\v	p ig) by @thm-matrix-multiplication-properties. By @thm-det-multiplicative and @thm-matrix-determinant-lemma applied to the vectors A^{-1}\u and \v, \det(A + \u\v	p) = \det A\,(1 + \v	p A^{-1}\u). (b) \det A 
e 0 by @thm-det-nonzero-iff-invertible, so \det(A + \u\v	p) 
e 0 exactly when 1 + \v	p A^{-1}\u 
e 0. Apply @thm-det-nonzero-iff-invertible again. (c) Take A = I_2, \u = (-1, 0), \v = (1, 0). Then \v	p\u = -1, and indeed A + \u\v	p =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} is not invertible.

title: 6.9 Orientation and Volume
content:
Orientation and Volume The chapter began in §1 with a picture: the area of a parallelogram, with a sign attached, obeys a few simple rules, and those rules pinned down ad - bc. We have since built the determinant in every size from the same rules. It is time to return to geometry and say precisely what the determinant measures. There are two halves to the answer. Its absolute value measures volume, and its sign measures orientation, the difference between a left hand and a right hand. Both halves need care. “Volume” in 
R^7 has no meaning until someone defines it, and “orientation” has no meaning at all over 
C. Throughout this section the field is 
R. What should the volume of a parallelepiped be? For vectors \a_1, \dots, \a_n \in 
R^n, the parallelepiped they span is the set P(\a_1, \dots, \a_n) \coloneqq \{ t_1\a_1 + \dots + t_n\a_n : 0 \le t_i \le 1 	ext{ for every } i \}. For n = 2 it is the parallelogram with sides \a_1, \a_2 at the origin, and for n = 3 a slanted box. For n = 1 it is the segment from 0 to \a_1. We would like to say “its volume is \lvert \det egin{pmatrix} \a_1 & \cdots & \a_n \end{pmatrix} vert”. But a theorem needs two sides, and one side is missing: we have no definition of the volume of a subset of 
R^n. School geometry supplies one for n = 2 and n = 3 through “base times height”, and the proper general notion, Lebesgue measure, belongs to a course in measure theory. So we proceed honestly in three steps. We define the volume of a parallelepiped by the determinant. We prove that this is the only function obeying the rules that any reasonable notion of volume must obey. And we state, without proof, that it agrees with Lebesgue measure. The volume of a parallelepiped is the size of the determinant of its edge vectors. [Volume of a Parallelepiped] Let n \ge 1 and \a_1, \dots, \a_n \in 
R^n. The (n-dimensional) volume of the parallelepiped spanned by \a_1, \dots, \a_n is \vol(\a_1, \dots, \a_n) \coloneqq  ig\lvert \det egin{pmatrix} \a_1 & \a_2 & \cdots & \a_n \end{pmatrix}  igvert \ \ge 0 . In words: stack the n edge vectors as the columns of a square matrix, take its determinant, and forget the sign. There must be exactly n vectors in 
R^n, so that the matrix is square. Examples. - The unit cube P(\e_1, \dots, \e_n) has volume \lvert \det I_n vert = 1. - A box with edges d_1\e_1, \dots, d_n\e_n has volume \lvert \det\diag(d_1, \dots, d_n) vert = \lvert d_1 \cdots d_n vert by @thm-det-triangular: the product of its side lengths, as it should be. - The parallelepiped spanned by (1, 2, 0), (0, 1, 1), (1, 0, 3) in 
R^3 has volume \left\lvert \det egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 \ 2 & 1 & 0 \ 0 & 1 & 3 \end{pmatrix} ightvert = \lvert 1\cdot(3 - 0) - 0 + 1\cdot(2 - 0) vert = 5, expanding along the first row. - Degenerate case. If \a_1, \dots, \a_n are linearly dependent, the parallelepiped is flattened into a proper subspace, and its volume is 0 by @thm-alternating-properties. For n = 2, P((1, 2), (2, 4)) is the segment from (0, 0) to (3, 6), with area \lvert 4 - 4 vert = 0. This case matters: “volume zero” is the geometric face of “not invertible”. Non-example by minimal change. Drop one vector: (1, 2, 0) and (0, 1, 1) span a genuine parallelogram in 
R^3, but the matrix  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 2 & 1 \ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} is 3 	imes 2 and has no determinant. The clause that fails is exactly n vectors in 
R^n. The 3-dimensional volume of that flat parallelogram would be 0, and its area needs a different formula (@exr-orientation-and-volume-c1). Why this definition. Reordering the vectors multiplies the determinant by a sign (@thm-alternating-properties), which the absolute value removes, so the volume does not depend on the order in which the edges are listed. The absolute value is also what makes volume non-negative. The sign we threw away is not garbage: it is the orientation, the subject of the second half of this section. Volume is not linear. Scaling one edge by 2 doubles the volume, but scaling the whole parallelepiped by 2 multiplies it by 2^n: \vol(2\a_1, \dots, 2\a_n) = \lvert \det(2A) vert = 2^n \vol(\a_1, \dots, \a_n), where A has columns \a_1, \dots, \a_n. A cube of side 2 in 
R^3 has volume 8, not 2; this failure persists even with the sign kept, since \det is linear in each edge separately, not in all edges at once. The absolute value also destroys additivity in a single edge: \vol(\a_1 +  _1, \a_2, \dots) is in general not \vol(\a_1, \a_2, \dots) + \vol( _1, \a_2, \dots): with \a_1 = \e_1,  _1 = -\e_1 in 
R^2 and \a_2 = \e_2, the left side is 0 and the right side is 2. Volume is forced by its rules Why should anyone accept @def-parallelepiped-volume? Because of what any notion of volume of parallelepipeds must satisfy. The pictures in §1 showed three facts about area, and they have obvious n-dimensional versions: stretching one edge by a factor c multiplies the volume by \lvert c vert; sliding one edge parallel to another (a shear) does not change the volume; and the unit cube has volume 1. The next theorem says that these three rules alone determine the volume completely. So any definition that obeys them, whether from school geometry or from measure theory, must agree with ours. [Volume Is Determined by Its Rules] Let n \ge 1, and let g be a function assigning a real number g(\a_1, \dots, \a_n) to every list of n vectors in 
R^n. Suppose that for every list, every i 
e j and every c \in 
R: 1. g(\a_1, \dots, c\a_i, \dots, \a_n) = \lvert c vert\, g(\a_1, \dots, \a_i, \dots, \a_n) (only slot i changes); 2. g(\a_1, \dots, \a_i + c\a_j, \dots, \a_n) = g(\a_1, \dots, \a_i, \dots, \a_n) (only slot i changes); 3. g(\e_1, \dots, \e_n) = 1. Then g(\a_1, \dots, \a_n) = \vol(\a_1, \dots, \a_n) for every list. Moreover, \vol itself satisfies (V1)–(V3). Think of g as a function of the matrix M with columns \a_1, \dots, \a_n. ① If the columns are dependent, shear one column to \0 and scale by 0: g = 0. ② Each elementary column operation changes g by the factor \lvert \det E vert. Scaling and shearing are (V1) and (V2); a swap is not among the rules, but three shears and a sign change perform it. ③ An invertible M is a product of elementary matrices, so peel them off one at a time until only I is left. For M \in M_n(
R) with columns \a_1, \dots, \a_n, write h(M) = g(\a_1, \dots, \a_n). Step 1: dependent columns give h(M) = 0. Suppose the columns are linearly dependent. By @thm-linear-dependence-lemma, some \a_i = c_1\a_1 + \dots + c_{i-1}\a_{i-1} (for i = 1, \a_1 = \0). Applying (V2) to slot i with the scalars -c_1, \dots, -c_{i-1}, one at a time, does not change g, and it replaces \a_i by \0 while the other slots stay fixed. Then (V1) with c = 0 gives g(\dots, \0, \dots) = g(\dots, 0 \cdot \0, \dots) = 0 \cdot g(\dots, \0, \dots) = 0. Hence h(M) = 0. Step 2: h(ME) = \lvert \det E vert\, h(M) for every elementary matrix E. By @thm-row-op-is-left-multiplication and @thm-transpose-properties, ME = (E	p M	p)	p, and E	p is the elementary matrix P_{ij}, D_i(c) or I + cE_{ji} when E is P_{ij}, D_i(c) or I + cE_{ij}. So right multiplication by E performs a column operation: swap columns i and j; multiply column i by c 
e 0; or add c times column i to column j. The determinants are \det P_{ij} = -1, \det D_i(c) = c and \det(I + cE_{ij}) = 1 by @thm-det-row-operations. - For E = I + cE_{ij}, (V2) gives h(ME) = h(M) = \lvert 1 vert\, h(M). - For E = D_i(c), (V1) gives h(ME) = \lvert c vert\, h(M). - For E = P_{ij}, watch only slots i and j, holding \x and \y. By (V2) three times, (\x, \y) 	o (\x + \y, \y) 	o (\x + \y, -\x) 	o (\y, -\x) leaves g unchanged, where the second step subtracts slot i from slot j and the third adds slot j to slot i. By (V1) with c = -1 on slot j, g at (\y, \x) equals \lvert -1 vert times g at (\y, -\x). Hence h(MP_{ij}) = h(M) = \lvert -1 vert\, h(M). Step 3: conclusion. If the columns of M are dependent, then h(M) = 0 by Step 1 and \det M = 0 by @thm-alternating-properties, so h(M) = \lvert \det M vert. Otherwise M is invertible by @thm-invertible-tfae, hence M = E_1E_2\cdots E_k is a product of elementary matrices by the same theorem. Applying Step 2 k times, starting from I, and then (V3), h(M) = h(IE_1\cdots E_k) = \lvert \det E_1 vert \cdots \lvert \det E_k vert\, h(I) = \lvert \det(E_1\cdots E_k) vert = \lvert \det M vert, where the third equality uses @thm-det-multiplicative and \lvert xy vert = \lvert x vert \lvert y vert. This proves g = \vol. Finally, \vol satisfies (V1) because the determinant is linear in each column (@thm-leibniz-formula-alternating) and \lvert c\,d vert = \lvert c vert \lvert d vert; (V2) by @thm-alternating-properties; and (V3) because \det I_n = 1. Agreement with area and volume from school. For n = 2, let g(\a_1, \a_2) be the area of the parallelogram P(\a_1, \a_2) in the sense of school geometry, base times height. The pictures of §1 are exactly (V1)–(V3) for this g: stretching a side by c stretches the base or the height by \lvert c vert; a shear \a_1 \mapsto \a_1 + c\a_2 slides the opposite side along a line parallel to the base \a_2, keeping base and height; and the unit square has area 1. Hence, by @thm-volume-characterization, school area equals \lvert \det egin{pmatrix} \a_1 & \a_2 \end{pmatrix} vert. For n = 3 the same argument works with “area of base times height”. What the theorem cannot supply is the geometric input itself: it takes the three rules as given. Agreement with Lebesgue measure. In measure theory, every reasonable subset S \subseteq 
R^n has an n-dimensional volume, its Lebesgue measure. One can prove that the Lebesgue measure of P(\a_1, \dots, \a_n) satisfies (V1)–(V3), and hence equals \vol(\a_1, \dots, \a_n). We state this without proof; nothing in this book depends on it. Which of the rules (V1)–(V3) does the function g(\a_1, \a_2) = \lvert \det egin{pmatrix} \a_1 & \a_2 \end{pmatrix} vert^2 on 
R^2 break? It satisfies (V2), since shears do not change the determinant, and (V3), since 1^2 = 1. It breaks (V1): g(2\e_1, \e_2) = 4, while \lvert 2 vert\, g(\e_1, \e_2) = 2. So the theorem does not apply, and indeed g 
e \vol. Linear maps scale volume Applying a linear map to a parallelepiped gives another parallelepiped: by linearity, T ig(\sum t_i\a_i ig) = \sum t_iT\a_i, so T(P(\a_1, \dots, \a_n)) = P(T\a_1, \dots, T\a_n). How does the volume change? Multiplicativity answers this in one line, and the answer does not depend on the parallelepiped. [Linear Maps Scale Volume by \lvert \det vert] Let T \in \cL(
R^n) and \a_1, \dots, \a_n \in 
R^n. Then \vol(T\a_1, \dots, T\a_n) = \lvert \det T vert \cdot \vol(\a_1, \dots, \a_n). In particular, the image of the unit cube under T has volume \lvert \det T vert. Let B be the matrix of T in the standard basis, so T\x = B\x for all \x (@thm-matrix-of-map-coordinates) and \det T = \det B (@def-det-operator). Let A =  egin{pmatrix} \a_1 & \cdots & \a_n \end{pmatrix}. By @thm-three-views-of-product, BA =  egin{pmatrix} B\a_1 & \cdots & B\a_n \end{pmatrix}. By @thm-det-multiplicative, \vol(T\a_1, \dots, T\a_n) = \lvert \det(BA) vert = \lvert \det B vert\,\lvert \det A vert = \lvert \det T vert\,\vol(\a_1, \dots, \a_n). For the unit cube take \a_i = \e_i, with \vol(\e_1, \dots, \e_n) = 1. This is the meaning of the determinant of a real operator: the factor by which it scales every volume. An operator with \det T = 0 squashes 
R^n into a lower-dimensional subspace, where n-dimensional volume is 0. In multivariable calculus the same fact, applied to the linear approximation of a smooth map, becomes the Jacobian factor \lvert \det J vert in the change-of-variables formula for integrals. [Area of an Image] Let T \colon 
R^2 	o 
R^2 be T(x, y) = (3x + y,\ x + 2y). Find the area of the image of the unit square, and of the image of the parallelogram P((1, 1), (-1, 2)). The standard matrix is B =  egin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 \ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}, with \det T = 6 - 1 = 5. By @thm-det-volume-scaling the image of the unit square, the parallelogram spanned by (3, 1) and (1, 2), has area 5. The parallelogram P((1, 1), (-1, 2)) has area \lvert 2 + 1 vert = 3, so its image has area 5 \cdot 3 = 15. Check directly: T(1, 1) = (4, 3) and T(-1, 2) = (-1, 3), and \lvert \det egin{pmatrix} 4 & -1 \ 3 & 3 \end{pmatrix} vert = \lvert 12 + 3 vert = 15. Orientation Now the sign. In 
R^2, the ordered basis (\e_1, \e_2) turns counterclockwise from its first vector to its second, while (\e_2, \e_1) turns clockwise. No rotation carries one arrangement to the other: a rotation of the plane keeps counterclockwise turns counterclockwise. The determinant sees the difference: \det egin{pmatrix} \e_1 & \e_2 \end{pmatrix} = 1 > 0 and \det egin{pmatrix} \e_2 & \e_1 \end{pmatrix} = -1 < 0. To compare two bases of an arbitrary real space, we compare them with each other rather than with a fixed standard basis, using the change-of-coordinates matrix of Chapter 3. Two bases have the same orientation when the matrix converting one into the other has positive determinant. Orientation Let V be a vector space over 
R with \dim V = n \ge 1, and let \sB and \sC be ordered bases of V. We say \sB and \sC have the same orientation if \det \mtx{\id}{\sB}{\sC} > 0, and opposite orientations if \det\mtx{\id}{\sB}{\sC} < 0. In words: write each vector of \sB in coordinates with respect to \sC, put the coordinate columns side by side (@def-change-of-coordinates-matrix), and look at the sign of the determinant. Exactly one of the two cases occurs, because \mtx{\id}{\sB}{\sC} is invertible (@thm-change-of-coordinates (c)), so its determinant is non-zero (@thm-det-nonzero-iff-invertible), and a non-zero real number is either positive or negative. The bases must be ordered: reordering a basis can change the answer. For V = 
R^n there is a shortcut. If B and C are the matrices whose columns are the vectors of \sB and \sC, then \mtx{\id}{\sB}{\sE} = B and \mtx{\id}{\sC}{\sE} = C for the standard basis \sE. By @thm-change-of-coordinates (b) and (c), \mtx{\id}{\sB}{\sC} = C^{-1}B. Since \det C\,\det C^{-1} = \det I = 1 (@thm-det-multiplicative), \det\mtx{\id}{\sB}{\sC} = \det B / \det C. So \sB and \sC have the same orientation if and only if \det B and \det C have the same sign. Examples. - In 
R^2, (\e_1, \e_2) and (\e_2, \e_1) have opposite orientations: \det I_2 = 1 and \det egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} = -1. - In 
R^3, (\e_1, \e_2, \e_3) and (\e_2, \e_3, \e_1) have the same orientation. The second matrix is the permutation matrix of a 3-cycle, whose sign is (-1)^{3-1} = 1. A cyclic shift of three vectors is two swaps. - In V = 
R[x]_{\le 1}, the bases \sB = (1, x) and \sC = (x, 1 + x) have 1 = -x + (1 + x) and x = x + 0 \cdot (1 + x), so \mtx{\id}{\sB}{\sC} =  egin{pmatrix} -1 & 1 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, with determinant -1. They have opposite orientations. Orientation makes sense in any real space, with no picture at all. - Degenerate case, n = 1. Bases of 
R are single non-zero numbers (a), and \mtx{\id}{(a)}{(b)} = (a/b). So (a) and (b) have the same orientation exactly when a and b have the same sign. The two orientations of a line are its two directions. Non-example by minimal change. In 
R^2, (-\e_1, -\e_2) has the same orientation as (\e_1, \e_2): \det(-I_2) = 1, and indeed it is the rotation of (\e_1, \e_2) by a half-turn. Change only one sign, to (\e_1, -\e_2): the determinant becomes -1, and the orientation flips. What changed is the sign of the determinant, which is the whole content of the definition. In 
R^3, by contrast, -I_3 has determinant -1: negating all three vectors reverses orientation. Why this definition. Using the change-of-coordinates matrix, rather than the matrices B and C above, makes the definition work in every real space, including spaces like 
R[x]_{\le 1} that have no standard picture. Requiring \det > 0 rather than \det = 1 is what gives a coarse, two-valued answer: rescaling a basis vector by a positive number should not change its handedness. The payoff is that “same orientation” really sorts all bases into two families, as the pictures suggest. [There Are Exactly Two Orientations] Let V be a vector space over 
R with \dim V = n \ge 1. 1. “Having the same orientation” is an equivalence relation on the set of ordered bases of V. 2. It has exactly two equivalence classes. If \sB = (\v_1, \dots, \v_n), then \sB^- = (-\v_1, \v_2, \dots, \v_n) lies in the class not containing \sB. The three axioms are three facts about change-of-coordinates matrices: \mtx{\id}{\sB}{\sB} = I; the matrix back is the inverse; and matrices compose along a chain \sB 	o \sC 	o \sD. Determinants turn these into 1 > 0, 1/	ext{positive} > 0 and 	ext{positive} \cdot 	ext{positive} > 0. For “exactly two”, flipping one vector gives a second class, and “negative times negative is positive” shows there is no third. Write d(\sB, \sC) = \det\mtx{\id}{\sB}{\sC}. By @thm-change-of-coordinates (b) and @thm-det-multiplicative, for bases \sB, \sC, \sD, d(\sB, \sD) = d(\sC, \sD)\, d(\sB, \sC). 	ag{$\ast$} (a) Reflexive: \mtx{\id}{\sB}{\sB} = I_n, so d(\sB, \sB) = 1 > 0. Symmetric: by (\ast) with \sD = \sB, d(\sC, \sB)\,d(\sB, \sC) = d(\sB, \sB) = 1, so d(\sC, \sB) = 1/d(\sB, \sC), which is positive when d(\sB, \sC) is. Transitive: if d(\sB, \sC) > 0 and d(\sC, \sD) > 0, then d(\sB, \sD) > 0 by (\ast), since a product of positive reals is positive. By @def-equivalence-relation, this is an equivalence relation. (b) At least two classes. \sB^- is a basis, and \mtx{\id}{\sB^-}{\sB} = \diag(-1, 1, \dots, 1), because -\v_1 = (-1)\v_1 and \v_j = 1 \cdot \v_j. Its determinant is -1 by @thm-det-triangular. So d(\sB^-, \sB) < 0, and \sB^- and \sB lie in different classes. At most two classes. Let \sC and \sD be bases, neither of which has the same orientation as \sB. Then d(\sC, \sB) < 0 and d(\sD, \sB) < 0, and by symmetry d(\sB, \sD) < 0 as well. By (\ast), d(\sC, \sD) = d(\sB, \sD)\,d(\sC, \sB) is a product of two negative reals, hence positive. So all bases outside the class of \sB lie in one class, and there are exactly two classes. Choosing one of the two classes is called orienting V; its bases are then called positively oriented, and the others negatively oriented. On 
R^n the standard choice is the class of (\e_1, \dots, \e_n). By the shortcut above, (\a_1, \dots, \a_n) is positively oriented if and only if \det egin{pmatrix} \a_1 & \cdots & \a_n \end{pmatrix} > 0. So the determinant of a real square matrix carries two independent pieces of information: its absolute value is a volume, and its sign is an orientation. Orientation needs 
R. The proof used two facts about the reals: every non-zero number is positive or negative, and products and inverses of positive numbers are positive. Over 
C there is no such splitting. Suppose we tried “\sB and \sC have the same orientation if d(\sB, \sC) has positive real part”. In 
C^1, with z = e^{i\pi/3}, the bases (\e_1), (z\e_1), (z^2\e_1) give d((\e_1), (z\e_1)) = z^{-1} and d((z\e_1), (z^2\e_1)) = z^{-1}, both with real part  rac12 > 0, but d((\e_1), (z^2\e_1)) = z^{-2} has real part - rac12: transitivity fails. Over 
F_2, -1 = 1, so the second basis \sB^- of the proof is \sB itself. The theorem holds verbatim over any field with a compatible order, such as 
Q, but not over 
C or a finite field. Do ((1, 2), (3, 4)) and ((3, 4), (1, 2)) have the same orientation? Does ((1, 2), (3, 4)) have the standard orientation of 
R^2? \det egin{pmatrix} 1 & 3 \ 2 & 4 \end{pmatrix} = 4 - 6 = -2 and \det egin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 \ 4 & 2 \end{pmatrix} = 6 - 4 = 2. The signs differ, so the two bases have opposite orientations. The first has negative determinant, so it is negatively oriented: it is not in the class of (\e_1, \e_2). The right-hand rule In 
R^3, the standard orientation is the one described by the right hand: curl the fingers of the right hand from the first basis vector toward the second, and the thumb points along the third. For (\e_1, \e_2, \e_3) with the usual picture of the axes, this is the familiar arrangement below. The cross product of \a = (a_1, a_2, a_3) and   = (b_1, b_2, b_3) in 
R^3 is \a 	imes   \coloneqq (a_2b_3 - a_3b_2,\ a_3b_1 - a_1b_3,\ a_1b_2 - a_2b_1). Physics defines it by the right-hand rule. Here is the linear-algebra reason the two descriptions match: (\a,  , \a 	imes  ) is always positively oriented. Expand \det egin{pmatrix} \a &   & \a 	imes   \end{pmatrix} along its third column (@thm-laplace-expansion). The cofactors of that column are C_{13} = a_2b_3 - a_3b_2, C_{23} = -(a_1b_3 - a_3b_1) and C_{33} = a_1b_2 - a_2b_1, which are exactly the three components of \a 	imes  . Hence \det egin{pmatrix} \a &   & \a 	imes   \end{pmatrix} = (a_2b_3 - a_3b_2)^2 + (a_3b_1 - a_1b_3)^2 + (a_1b_2 - a_2b_1)^2 \ \ge\ 0 . If \a and   are linearly independent, the 3 	imes 2 matrix  egin{pmatrix} \a &   \end{pmatrix} has rank 2, so one of its 2 	imes 2 minors, which are \pm the components of \a 	imes  , is non-zero (@thm-rank-via-minors). Then the determinant is strictly positive, so (\a,  , \a 	imes  ) is a basis (@thm-det-nonzero-iff-invertible) with the standard orientation. For example, \e_1 	imes \e_2 = (0, 0, 1) = \e_3, matching the picture. Orientation-preserving maps An invertible operator carries each basis to a basis. Does it keep the orientation? The answer is the same for every basis and depends only on the sign of \det T. [Determinant Sign and Orientation] Let V be a vector space over 
R with \dim V = n \ge 1, let T \in \cL(V) be invertible, and let \sB = (\v_1, \dots, \v_n) be any basis of V. Then T\sB = (T\v_1, \dots, T\v_n) is a basis of V, and \mtx{\id}{T\sB}{\sB} = [T]_{\sB}. Hence \sB and T\sB have the same orientation if and only if \det T > 0, and this does not depend on \sB. Since T is invertible, it is an isomorphism, so T\sB is a basis by @thm-isomorphism-preserves-bases. By @def-change-of-coordinates-matrix, column j of \mtx{\id}{T\sB}{\sB} is \coord{T\v_j}{\sB}, which is column j of [T]_{\sB} by @def-matrix-of-linear-map. Hence the two matrices are equal, and by @def-det-operator, \det\mtx{\id}{T\sB}{\sB} = \det T. By @def-orientation and the symmetry in @thm-two-orientations (a), \sB and T\sB have the same orientation exactly when \det T > 0. An invertible operator with \det T > 0 is orientation-preserving, and one with \det T < 0 is orientation-reversing. Rotations of the plane preserve orientation and reflections reverse it (@exr-orientation-and-volume-c2). In 
R^3, the map \x \mapsto -\x reverses orientation, since \det(-I_3) = -1: a right hand, pushed through the origin, becomes a left hand. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. State the definition of the volume of the parallelepiped spanned by \a_1, \dots, \a_n \in 
R^n, and say what it is when the vectors are dependent. 2. True or false: \vol(\a_1 +  , \a_2, \dots, \a_n) = \vol(\a_1, \dots, \a_n) + \vol( , \a_2, \dots, \a_n). Justify your answer. 3. Which three rules characterize volume in @thm-volume-characterization? 4. True or false: if \det T = -2, then T doubles every volume. Justify your answer. 5. Define “same orientation” for two ordered bases of a real vector space. 6. True or false: for every n \ge 1, the map \x \mapsto -\x on 
R^n reverses orientation. Justify your answer. (a) \vol(\a_1, \dots, \a_n) = \lvert \det egin{pmatrix} \a_1 & \cdots & \a_n \end{pmatrix} vert (@def-parallelepiped-volume). For dependent vectors it is 0, by @thm-alternating-properties. (b) False. With n = 2, \a_1 = \e_1,   = -\e_1, \a_2 = \e_2: the left side is \vol(\0, \e_2) = 0, the right side is 1 + 1 = 2. The absolute value destroys additivity. (c) (V1) scaling one vector by c scales the volume by \lvert c vert; (V2) adding a multiple of one vector to another does not change it; (V3) the unit cube has volume 1. (d) True. By @thm-det-volume-scaling, \vol(T\a_1, \dots, T\a_n) = \lvert -2 vert \vol(\a_1, \dots, \a_n). The sign only affects orientation. (e) \sB and \sC have the same orientation if \det\mtx{\id}{\sB}{\sC} > 0 (@def-orientation). (f) False. \det(-I_n) = (-1)^n, so by @prp-orientation-preserving the map reverses orientation for odd n and preserves it for even n. In 
R^2 it is the rotation by a half-turn. B. Practice [B1: Volume of a parallelepiped] Find the volume of the parallelepiped in 
R^3 spanned by (2, 1, 0), (1, 3, 1) and (0, 1, 1). Hence find the volume of its image under the map T(x, y, z) = (x + y,\ y + z,\ 2z). Expanding along the first row, \det egin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & 0 \ 1 & 3 & 1 \ 0 & 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = 2(3 - 1) - 1\cdot(1 - 0) + 0 = 3, so the volume is 3. The standard matrix of T is  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 0 \ 0 & 1 & 1 \ 0 & 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}, upper triangular with determinant 2 (@thm-det-triangular). By @thm-det-volume-scaling the image has volume 2 \cdot 3 = 6. [B2: Comparing orientations] In 
R^3, let \sB = ((1, 1, 0), (0, 1, 1), (1, 0, 1)), \sC = ((0, 1, 0), (1, 0, 0), (1, 1, 1)) and \sD = ((1, 0, 1), (1, 1, 0), (0, 1, 1)). Determine which pairs have the same orientation, and which are positively oriented. Justify your answer. By the shortcut after @def-orientation, compare signs of the determinants of the matrices with these columns. Expanding along the first row: \det egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 \ 1 & 1 & 0 \ 0 & 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = 1\cdot(1 - 0) - 0 + 1\cdot(1 - 0) = 2, \qquad \det egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 & 1 \ 1 & 0 & 1 \ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = -1, the second by expanding along the last row: 1 \cdot \det egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} = -1. The list \sD is \sB shifted cyclically, ( _3,  _1,  _2); moving the last column to the front takes two column swaps, so by @thm-alternating-properties its determinant is (-1)^2 \cdot 2 = 2. Hence \sB and \sD are positively oriented and have the same orientation; \sC is negatively oriented, opposite to both. [B3: Areas of images] Let T(x, y) = (2x + y,\ -x + 3y) on 
R^2. 1. Find the area of the image of the unit square under T. 2. Find the area of the image of the parallelogram P((1, 0), (1, 2)), first by @thm-det-volume-scaling and then directly. 3. Is T orientation-preserving? (a) The standard matrix  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \ -1 & 3 \end{pmatrix} has determinant 6 + 1 = 7, so the image of the unit square has area 7. (b) \vol((1, 0), (1, 2)) = \lvert \det egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix} vert = 2, so the image has area 7 \cdot 2 = 14. Directly, T(1, 0) = (2, -1) and T(1, 2) = (4, 5), and \lvert \det egin{pmatrix} 2 & 4 \ -1 & 5 \end{pmatrix} vert = \lvert 10 + 4 vert = 14. (c) Yes: \det T = 7 > 0, so by @prp-orientation-preserving T preserves orientation. C. Going deeper [C1: Area of a triangle in space] For \u, \v \in 
R^3, let A =  egin{pmatrix} \u & \v \end{pmatrix} \in M_{3 	imes 2}(
R). We define the area of the parallelogram P(\u, \v) \subseteq 
R^3 to be \sqrt{\det(A	p A)}; Chapter 10 justifies this with inner products. 1. Show that \det(A	p A) \ge 0, so the square root exists, and that \det(A	p A) = (u_2v_3 - u_3v_2)^2 + (u_3v_1 - u_1v_3)^2 + (u_1v_2 - u_2v_1)^2. 2. Show that if \u and \v lie in the plane z = 0, this area equals the area \vol((u_1, u_2), (v_1, v_2)) of @def-parallelepiped-volume in 
R^2. 3. Find the area of the triangle with vertices (1, 0, 0), (0, 2, 0), (0, 0, 3). Hint: apply @cor-gram-determinant-nonnegative to A	p. (a) A	p \in M_{2 	imes 3}(
R) and (A	p)	p = A, so by @cor-gram-determinant-nonnegative applied to A	p, \det(A	p A) = \sum_{|S| = 2} (\det (A	p)_{[2],S})^2 \ge 0. The 2 	imes 2 minors of A	p =  egin{pmatrix} u_1 & u_2 & u_3 \ v_1 & v_2 & v_3 \end{pmatrix} are u_1v_2 - u_2v_1, u_1v_3 - u_3v_1, u_2v_3 - u_3v_2 for S = \{1,2\}, \{1,3\}, \{2,3\}; squaring removes the signs, giving the stated sum. (b) If u_3 = v_3 = 0, two of the three squares vanish, and \det(A	p A) = (u_1v_2 - u_2v_1)^2. Hence \sqrt{\det(A	p A)} = \lvert u_1v_2 - u_2v_1 vert = \lvert \det egin{pmatrix} u_1 & v_1 \ u_2 & v_2 \end{pmatrix} vert, which is \vol((u_1, u_2), (v_1, v_2)). (c) The triangle is half of the parallelogram spanned by \u = (0, 2, 0) - (1, 0, 0) = (-1, 2, 0) and \v = (0, 0, 3) - (1, 0, 0) = (-1, 0, 3). By (a), \det(A	p A) = (6 - 0)^2 + (0 + 3)^2 + (0 + 2)^2 = 36 + 9 + 4 = 49. As a check, A	p A =  egin{pmatrix} 5 & 1 \ 1 & 10 \end{pmatrix} has determinant 50 - 1 = 49. So the parallelogram has area 7, and the triangle has area  rac72. [C2: Rotations and reflections] For 	heta \in 
R, let R_	heta =  egin{pmatrix} \cos	heta & -\sin	heta \ \sin	heta & \cos	heta \end{pmatrix} (rotation by 	heta) and S_	heta =  egin{pmatrix} \cos 2	heta & \sin 2	heta \ \sin 2	heta & -\cos 2	heta \end{pmatrix} (reflection in the line through 0 at angle 	heta). 1. Show that every rotation preserves orientation and area, and every reflection reverses orientation and preserves area. 2. Show that S_	heta S_\varphi is orientation-preserving for all 	heta, \varphi. (It is in fact a rotation, but you need not show this.) 3. Prove that no M \in M_2(
R) satisfies M^2 = S_0 = \diag(1, -1). Does the same argument rule out M^2 = -I_2? (a) \det R_	heta = \cos^2	heta + \sin^2	heta = 1 > 0 and \det S_	heta = -\cos^2 2	heta - \sin^2 2	heta = -1 < 0. By @prp-orientation-preserving, rotations preserve and reflections reverse orientation. Both have \lvert \det vert = 1, so both preserve area by @thm-det-volume-scaling. (b) By @thm-det-multiplicative, \det(S_	heta S_\varphi) = (-1)(-1) = 1 > 0. (c) If M^2 = S_0, then (\det M)^2 = \det S_0 = -1 by @thm-det-multiplicative, impossible for a real number \det M. The argument says nothing about -I_2, since \det(-I_2) = 1; and indeed R_{\pi/2}^2 = R_{\pi/2}R_{\pi/2} =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}^2 = -I_2. An orientation-reversing map can never be the square of a real map, since the square of anything preserves orientation.

title: 6.10 The Characteristic Polynomial
content:
The Characteristic Polynomial For a square matrix A over F and a scalar c \in F, when is cI - A invertible? The question matters: cI - A fails to be invertible exactly when A\v = c\v for some non-zero vector \v, the situation Chapter 8 is built around. The determinant answers the question for each single c. This section lets c vary. Replacing the number c by a variable x turns \det(cI - A) into a polynomial, the characteristic polynomial, and the scalars we are looking for become its roots. The price is that xI - A is a matrix of polynomials, not of field elements, so we must check which determinant facts survive there. The remarks at the ends of §4, §5 and §6 did exactly that bookkeeping, and here we cash them in. From a number to a variable Take A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \ 3 & 4 \end{pmatrix} \in M_2(
Q). For each c \in 
Q, \det(cI - A) = \det egin{pmatrix} c - 1 & -2 \ -3 & c - 4 \end{pmatrix} = (c - 1)(c - 4) - 6 = c^2 - 5c - 2 . The same expression c^2 - 5c - 2 appears whatever c is. It is the value at c of one polynomial, and that polynomial deserves a name. To define it directly, without first choosing c, we put the variable x into the matrix and take the determinant of xI - A =  egin{pmatrix} x - 1 & -2 \ -3 & x - 4 \end{pmatrix}, a matrix whose entries lie in F[x]. Is that allowed? F[x] is not a field, but it is a commutative ring in the sense of the remark in §4: all the field axioms hold except the existence of inverses (@thm-polynomial-ring-laws). The Leibniz formula of @def-determinant uses only sums, differences and products of entries, so it defines \det M \in F[x] for every M \in M_n(F[x]). The characteristic polynomial of A is the determinant of xI - A, computed with polynomial entries. [Characteristic Polynomial] Let n \ge 1 and A = (a_{ij}) \in M_n(F). The characteristic polynomial of A is p_A(x) \coloneqq \det(xI_n - A) = \sum_{\sigma \in S_n} \sgn(\sigma) \prod_{j=1}^{n}  ig(x\,\delta_{\sigma(j)j} - a_{\sigma(j)j} ig) \ \in F[x], where \delta_{ij} = 1 if i = j and 0 otherwise, so that x\delta_{ij} - a_{ij} is the (i, j)-entry of xI_n - A. The determinant is the Leibniz sum of @def-determinant, computed in the commutative ring F[x]. In words: subtract A from x times the identity, so that x appears only on the diagonal; then take the determinant exactly as for a matrix of numbers, multiplying and adding polynomials instead of scalars. The result is one polynomial, not a number. Well-definedness. Each term of the Leibniz sum is a product of n polynomials, and the sum is finite, so p_A is a polynomial. It depends only on A. How to compute it. By the remarks in §4, §5 and §6, the following results were proved without dividing, and so hold for matrices over F[x]: @thm-det-transpose and @thm-det-triangular (§4), @thm-det-multiplicative by its first proof (§5), @thm-laplace-expansion (§6), and @thm-det-block-triangular (§8). So we may expand \det(xI - A) along any row or column, and read it off from triangular or block triangular shape. What we may not do is row reduce xI - A by dividing by a polynomial entry, as the warning below explains. Examples. - 1 	imes 1. For A = (a), p_A(x) = x - a. - 2 	imes 2. For A =  egin{pmatrix} a & b \ c & d \end{pmatrix}, p_A(x) = (x - a)(x - d) - bc = x^2 - (a + d)x + (ad - bc) = x^2 - (	r A)\,x + \det A . For A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \ 3 & 4 \end{pmatrix} this is x^2 - 5x - 2, as above. - Triangular. If A is upper or lower triangular, so is xI - A, with diagonal entries x - a_{ii}. By @thm-det-triangular over F[x], p_A(x) = (x - a_{11})(x - a_{22})\cdots(x - a_{nn}). - Degenerate cases. The zero matrix has p_{0}(x) = x^n, and the identity has p_{I_n}(x) = (x - 1)^n; both are triangular. These two polynomials are different, although both matrices are as simple as possible, which already shows that p_A records something about A. [A 3 	imes 3 Characteristic Polynomial] Find p_A for A =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 & 1 \ 1 & 3 & 1 \ 1 & 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix} \in M_3(
Q). We have xI - A =  egin{pmatrix} x - 2 & 0 & -1 \ -1 & x - 3 & -1 \ -1 & 0 & x - 2 \end{pmatrix}. Column 2 has a single non-zero entry, x - 3 in position (2, 2). Expanding along it (@thm-laplace-expansion over F[x]), p_A(x) = (x - 3)\,(-1)^{2+2}\det egin{pmatrix} x - 2 & -1 \ -1 & x - 2 \end{pmatrix} = (x - 3) ig((x - 2)^2 - 1 ig) = (x - 1)(x - 3)^2 . Then A^2 =  egin{pmatrix} a^2 + bc & ab + bd \ ca + dc & bc + d^2 \end{pmatrix} and (a + d)A =  egin{pmatrix} a^2 + ad & ab + bd \ ac + dc & ad + d^2 \end{pmatrix}. The difference is  egin{pmatrix} bc - ad & 0 \ 0 & bc - ad \end{pmatrix} = -(\det A)I, as claimed. (c) By (a) and (b), A^2 = (	r A)A. By induction, A^m = (	r A)^{m-1}A for all m \ge 1: if it holds for m, then A^{m+1} = (	r A)^{m-1}A^2 = (	r A)^mA. If A = 0, then 	r A = 0. If A 
e 0, then 0 = A^k = (	r A)^{k-1}A forces (	r A)^{k-1} = 0, since a non-zero matrix times a scalar is zero only if the scalar is zero; here k \ge 2, because k = 1 would give A = 0. Hence 	r A = 0 by @thm-field-basic-properties (f), applied repeatedly. So p_A = x^2 - 0\cdot x + 0 = x^2, and A^2 = (	r A)A = 0. (d) A =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} has A^2 = 0 and A 
e 0. [C3: Odd size over the reals] Let n be odd and A \in M_n(
R). 1. Prove that there is c \in 
R and a non-zero \v \in 
R^n with A\v = c\v. 2. Show by an example that (a) fails for n = 2. 3. Show that (a) holds for every A \in M_n(
C) and every n \ge 1. (a) By @thm-charpoly-coefficients, p_A \in 
R[x] has odd degree n. By @cor-odd-degree-real-root, it has a real root c. By @thm-charpoly-root-iff-singular, there is a non-zero \v \in 
R^n with A\v = c\v. (b) The rotation R =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} has p_R = x^2 + 1, with no real root; by @thm-charpoly-root-iff-singular no real c and non-zero real \v satisfy R\v = c\v. (c) p_A \in
